cards.text:
Accounts and sign-in
====================

.. rst-class:: lead

   A central server knows who is asking. There are no passwords: you sign in
   with a link sent to your work email.
cards.heading: Accounts and sign-in

cards.text:
Single-user and central
-----------------------

A server started without settings, or with settings that have no ``[auth]``
table, is **single-user**: there's no sign-in and whoever opens it can do
everything, as on a laptop or in the demo.

A server with ``[auth]`` in its settings (``server --settings server.toml``)
is **central**: every page and API call needs a signed-in user, and things
people make (reports, scratch runs) are theirs.

.. code-block:: toml

   base_url = "https://automation.example.com"   # the address in emailed links

   [auth]
   allowed_domains = ["example.com"]   # who may sign in
   admins = ["lead@example.com"]       # who may administer
   session_days = 30                   # default; renewed while used
   link_minutes = 15                   # default; how long a link works

   [smtp]                              # without it, links are printed to the log
   host = "mail.example.com"
   port = 25
   starttls = false
   sender = "automation@example.com"
   # username and password, if the relay needs them; the password can come
   # from AUTOMATION_SMTP_PASSWORD instead
cards.heading: Single-user and central

cards.text:
Signing in
----------

#. Open any page. You're asked for your email address.
#. Anyone with an address at one of the ``allowed_domains`` gets a sign-in
   link by email. Their account is made the first time they sign in, with
   no admin needed.
#. The link works **once**, for ``link_minutes``. Opening it shows a
   **Sign in** button rather than signing you in straight away, so mail
   scanners that open links don't use them up.
#. You stay signed in for ``session_days``, and every visit renews that, so
   someone who uses the server at least monthly never signs in again.
   **Sign out** is on the Account page.

Without ``[smtp]`` (a server being tried out) the link is printed in the
server's log, ready to be copied.

Sessions are cookies that scripts on the page can't read, and that other
sites can't send with a form (``SameSite=Lax``). Set ``base_url`` to an
``https://`` address and the cookie is only ever sent over HTTPS.
cards.heading: Signing in

cards.text:
Devices
-------

The local client (see :doc:`local-client`) signs in with
``automation-v3 login --server URL``. That emails you a link too; opening it
asks you to **Approve** the device, and the client then keeps a token that
acts as you. Your **Account** page lists your devices, when each last
connected, and lets you remove any of them: its token stops working at
once.
cards.heading: Devices

cards.text:
Admins
------

Admins are the addresses in ``admins``. Being listed is checked on every
request, so a change to the settings takes effect when the server restarts,
and the settings' history shows who was an admin when. The **Admin** page
lists everyone who has signed in, and holds the tokens workers use (see
:doc:`workers`).
cards.heading: Admins

cards.text:
What is kept
------------

The database keeps each user's email, when they first signed in and when
they were last seen. Links, sessions and tokens are random secrets that are
shown or sent once; only their SHA-256 is stored, so a copy of the database
can't be used to sign in.
cards.heading: What is kept

cards.text:
Configuration management
========================

.. rst-class:: lead

   Every run records exactly what produced it, and a rerun either reproduces
   that or says it didn't.
cards.heading: Configuration management

cards.text:
What a run records
------------------

The closure
   The script and every ``core.rst`` and import it loaded, as checked in on
   the workspace's branch (edits not yet committed run only in
   :doc:`scratch`), copied into the run's ``closure/`` folder and hashed.
   Changing any of those files later doesn't change what the run says it
   ran.

The variation
   Its name and the values it bound.

UUT versions
   Each UUT's version id and digest, and whether the worker installed it or
   found it already installed.

The environment fingerprint
   What the environment plugin reports about itself (see
   :doc:`../blocks/uuts-and-environments`), plus the framework's own
   fingerprint: its version, its git commit and whether that checkout has
   uncommitted changes (a ``dev`` install).
cards.heading: What a run records

cards.text:
Identity -------- The **identity** of a run is a hash of: .. mermaid:: :caption: What a run's identity is made of flowchart LR closure["Closure hash
the script, its core.rst chain and imports"] --> identity variation["Variation values"] --> identity uuts["UUT versions and digests"] --> identity fingerprint["Fingerprint hash
environment facts, framework version and commit"] --> identity identity((Identity)):::accent Two runs with the same identity ran the same test text, the same way, on the same software, in an environment that reported the same facts. The run page shows the identity in its details.
cards.heading: Identity

cards.text:
Reruns ------ **Rerun** queues a run again exactly: the same stored closure (not the workspace as it is now), environment, variation and UUT versions, as a new run in the same report. If any live worker's environment has the original fingerprint, the rerun is **pinned** to such a worker, and gets the same identity. If none does, the environment has **drifted**. The rerun is refused, and the page shows, for each live worker, which fingerprint fields differ from the original. From there you can: - bring an environment back to the original configuration and rerun; or - choose **Rerun anyway**, which queues it unpinned and marks the new run :status:`not identical`, linked to the run it reran. .. mermaid:: :caption: A rerun reproduces the original, or says it can't flowchart TB rerun([Rerun]) --> match{{"A live worker's environment
has the original fingerprint?"}} match -- yes --> pinned["Queued, pinned to such a worker:
the stored closure, variation and versions"] pinned --> same[The same identity]:::success match -- no --> drifted["Refused: drifted
the page shows which fields differ"]:::warning drifted -- "an environment is brought back" --> match drifted -- Rerun anyway --> unpinned[Queued unpinned] unpinned --> other["not identical,
linked to the run it reran"]:::warning To test the current text of a script instead, add it to the report again rather than rerunning. .. note:: The framework's git commit is part of the fingerprint, so on a development checkout any new commit counts as drift. Whether dev installs should ignore the commit is an open question.
cards.heading: Reruns

cards.text:
Deployment
==========

.. rst-class:: lead

   One program, three ways to run it: a central server the team shares, a
   client on each person's machine, or a single-user server for working
   alone.
cards.heading: Deployment

cards.text:
The three modes --------------- .. mermaid:: :caption: A central server mirrors the team's repository; clients and workers connect to it flowchart LR subgraph desk [Each person's machine] worktree[("Git worktrees")] client["Client
CLI and local web UI"]:::accent builds[("Local builds")] end git([The team's git remote]):::ghost buildrepo([The build repository]):::ghost subgraph central [Central server] web["Web app and APIs"]:::accent mirror[("Mirror of the remote")] db[("Accounts, queue
sqlite")] reports[("reports/")] end subgraph lab [Lab] worker[Workers]:::accent end worktree -- push --> git git -- "webhook, fetch" --> mirror client -- reads --> worktree client -- "scratch uploads,
requirements" --> web client -- "pushes, with your
own credentials" --> buildrepo builds --> client worker -- "worker token" --> web worker -- "installers pull" --> buildrepo web --> mirror web --> db web --> reports **Central server** The team's server: ``automation-v3 server --settings server.toml``, with ``[auth]`` and ``[git]`` in the settings. Everyone signs in (see :doc:`accounts`). Scripts come from a mirror of the team's git remote. Reports run only what has been pushed, and record the commit they ran. Workers in the lab connect to it with worker tokens (see :doc:`workers`). **Client** On each person's machine (see :doc:`local-client`). It reads scripts in their own git worktrees, checks them as they're written, and runs them in scratch, on the central server's workers or on the machine itself. It uploads local builds of a UUT to the build repository. Requirements come from the central server. **Single-user server** ``automation-v3 server --workspace-path REPO`` with no settings, which is how it has always worked. Scripts come from the git worktrees of ``REPO``, there's no sign-in and nobody owns anything. It suits a laptop, a lab with one person, and the demo.
cards.heading: The three modes

cards.text:
Settings
--------

A central server's settings are a TOML file:

.. code-block:: toml

   base_url = "https://automation.example.com"

   [auth]
   allowed_domains = ["example.com"]
   admins = ["lead@example.com"]

   [smtp]
   host = "mail.example.com"
   sender = "automation@example.com"

   [git]
   remote = "git@git.example.com:team/scripts.git"
   webhook_secret = "a long random string"   # or AUTOMATION_WEBHOOK_SECRET
   # mirror_path = "mirror.git"              # default; relative to the database's folder

:doc:`accounts` describes ``[auth]`` and ``[smtp]``. An unknown setting is an
error at startup, so a misspelling doesn't quietly do nothing.
cards.heading: Settings

cards.text:
The mirror
----------

With ``[git]``, the server keeps a ``git clone --mirror`` of ``remote`` next to
its database, and every branch of the remote is a workspace, shown at its
latest commit. The server's own account needs read access to the remote
(for example a deploy key). It never pushes.

Nothing is edited on the server, so there are no in-work files: what you
see is what was pushed. To run something that isn't pushed yet, use
scratch from the client.

The mirror is kept current two ways:

**The webhook**
   Point the git host's push webhook at ``https://SERVER/hooks/git`` with
   ``webhook_secret`` as its secret. GitHub and Gitea sign the body
   (``X-Hub-Signature-256`` or ``X-Gitea-Signature``); GitLab sends the
   secret as ``X-Gitlab-Token``. Anything else is refused, and so is every
   webhook while no secret is set.

**Before queuing**
   Queuing a report fetches first, so "I just pushed" works even if a webhook
   was missed. Each addition and run records the commit it ran.

The server clones or fetches when it starts, and won't start if it can't.
cards.heading: The mirror

cards.text:
Running it
----------

- Put it behind a reverse proxy that terminates HTTPS, and set ``base_url``
  to the ``https://`` address. Emailed links use it, and session cookies are
  then only sent over HTTPS.
- One process serves one team (tens of users, a few dozen workers): sqlite
  in WAL mode and report folders on local disk are enough. Back up the
  database file and the reports folder together.
- Workers connect out to the server, so lab machines need no inbound access.
cards.heading: Running it

cards.text:
Editing scripts
===============

.. rst-class:: lead

   The workspace page opens files in tabs and edits them a part at a time,
   straight into your worktree.
cards.heading: Editing scripts

cards.text:
Where editing works
-------------------

The editor writes the files of a git worktree on the machine the app runs
on: a single-user server, or the :doc:`local client <local-client>`. Git
stays outside it: you commit and push as you do after editing in any other
editor. A central server shows what was pushed and doesn't edit.
cards.heading: Where editing works

cards.text:
Tabs
----

Picking a file in the tree opens it in a tab; a link to a script from
another page opens it in a tab too. The tabs you have open are remembered
for each workspace. A tab with edits that aren't saved has a dot.

Closing a tab with unsaved edits doesn't lose them: they are kept in the
browser, and come back when the file is opened again.
cards.heading: Tabs

cards.text:
Cards
-----

A script shows as it reads, cut into parts, each one a card:

Text
   A section of prose, from its heading to the next heading or block.
   It is edited as reStructuredText.

Block
   One ``rvt`` block. Editing it shows only its code: the ``.. rvt::``
   line, its options and the indentation are written for you.

Variant
   An ``rvt-variant``: text and blocks that are only for some variations,
   marked by a rule down their left. The cards inside it are ordinary
   cards.

Source
   A block or variant that can't be read is edited as the
   reStructuredText it is.

The page shows the script and nothing else. Pointing at a card shows two
marks to its left:

``..``
   The card's menu: add text or steps below (or above) it, edit it, move
   it up or down, delete it. For a block, also give it a title, make it a
   definitions block or a table, and say which variations it is for.
``::``
   Drag it: to another place, into a variant or out of one.

Click a card to edit its text. **Esc** or **Ctrl+Enter** closes it and keeps
what you typed; **Cancel** drops it.

**Double click a title** to change it where it is: a block's title, or a
section's heading. Enter keeps it, Esc leaves it as it was.
cards.heading: Cards

cards.text:
Variations
~~~~~~~~~~

Where a script declares variations, a block's menu has **Only for**: **All**,
and each variation. Pick one or more to limit the block to them; **All**
makes it for every variation again. Scripts that declare no variations
don't show it.

**Put in a variant**, in the menu, wraps a card in a variant, for text and
blocks that belong to the same variations; the variant's own menu picks
them, and **Take out of the variant** undoes it. Moving a card up or down
steps it into a variant next to it, or out of the one it is in.

**Undo** (Ctrl+Z) and **Redo** (Ctrl+Shift+Z) walk back and forth through
everything done to a tab's cards, in order: an edit, a move, a delete, a new
title. While a card is open, Ctrl+Z undoes typing in it.

Any other text file opens as one card of its text.
cards.heading: Variations

cards.text:
New scripts, clones and folders
-------------------------------

**New script**, above the tree, asks for a title, a file name (made from
the title unless you type one) and a folder. The script starts with its
title, a Requirements section and one block with a ``(TBD)`` step.

A requirement's page offers **Write a script for this**: the new script
then starts with the requirement's text and lists it under Requirements.

**File → Clone…** copies the open script under a new title, its
requirements included.

A new script or a clone opens as a tab with unsaved edits. Nothing is
written to the worktree until you save it, so one you abandon (**Discard
edits**) leaves no file behind. Until then it is kept in the browser, and
its tab comes back if the page is reloaded.

**File → Rename or move…** gives the open file another name or folder,
and **File → Delete…** removes it from the worktree; both act at once.
Reports that already ran a script keep the name it had then, and git can
bring back a deleted file that was committed.

**New folder** makes a folder, with a ``core.rst`` for the definitions its
scripts share if you ask for one.
cards.heading: New scripts, clones and folders

cards.text:
Saving
------

**Save** (Ctrl+S) writes the tab's file. **Run in scratch** runs the files
on disk, so it saves the script first; when files it loads have unsaved
edits in other tabs, it offers to save them too. Only the cards you edited are
rewritten: every other line of the file stays exactly as it was. **Discard
edits** drops a tab's unsaved edits and shows the file again.

A script is only cut into cards in the **In work** view with every
variation showing; pick a variation, or **Checked in**, to read it that way.
cards.heading: Saving

cards.text:
Errors and completion as you type
---------------------------------

**Problems**, above the tabs, lists every error and warning in the open
files and the files they load; picking one shows the card it is in. The
file tree counts the problems of each file too.

While a script is open, a language server checks it as its cards make it,
unsaved edits included, a moment after you stop typing. It reports what a
script's page reports: unknown names, wrong calls, code that can't be read.

- In the card being edited, the code at fault is underlined; hover it for
  the message.
- Every card lists its problems beneath it, and the tab counts the errors.
- A ``core.rst`` open in another tab is checked with: break a definition
  there and the scripts that use it say so before anything is saved.

In a block, **Ctrl+Space** completes the names it can use: blocks (offered
first after an opening parenthesis, with how they are called), builtins,
the definitions of the script and of its ``core.rst`` files, UUT handles,
variation values, and the parameters and ``let`` names around the cursor.
Completion also opens by itself as you type a name.

Hovering a name in a block says what it is: a block's calls and
documentation, a definition's code and the file it is in, a UUT handle, a
variation value with what each variation gives it. Where it can be told
without running anything, it also says what the name's value is: a literal,
or another name for one, and for a ref (or a path below one, such as
``nav.time``) its kind and full path; for a group, each member's.

While you type a call, the line under the editor shows how it is called,
with the argument you are on marked: a block's forms, or the parameters of a
function the script or a ``core.rst`` defines.

Below a ref, completion offers the paths that exist when its kind of ref
can say (see :doc:`../blocks/writing-blocks`): typing ``eps.`` after
``(def eps (connector "vm.eps"))`` offers ``soc``, ``charge-current`` and the
rest, and so does the path inside ``(connector "vm.``. A path that doesn't
exist is marked with a warning, as it is wherever a ref is made with one.
A warning, not an error: the script still queues, and fails when a run
reaches the path.

In prose, typing ``:req:`` and a backquote completes requirement ids, with
each requirement's text; hovering an id shows its text, and an id that isn't
in the requirements the workspace verifies is marked. Ids are only checked
when there are requirements to check against, and the local client, which
asks the central server for one requirement at a time, shows a
requirement's text on hover but can't list or check them.
cards.heading: Errors and completion as you type

cards.text:
In another editor
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The same server runs on its own as ``automation-v3 lsp``, speaking the
Language Server Protocol on stdin and stdout, so an editor with an LSP
client gets the same errors and completion. Start it for ``.rst`` files
with the worktree as the root; it takes the worktree's ``rvts`` folder as
the scripts root, and reads requirements from the database at ``--dbpath``
(``./automationv3.db`` unless you say) when it is there. In Neovim, for
example:

.. code-block:: lua

   vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd("FileType", {
     pattern = "rst",
     callback = function(args)
       vim.lsp.start({
         name = "automation-v3",
         cmd = { "automation-v3", "lsp" },
         root_dir = vim.fs.root(args.buf, { "rvts", ".git" }),
       })
     end,
   })
cards.heading: In another editor

cards.text:
When the file changes on disk
-----------------------------

A checkout, a pull or another editor can change a file that is open in a
tab. The editor checks when the window gets the focus back and before every
save.

A tab without unsaved edits just shows the new file. A tab with unsaved
edits says the file changed and offers:

**See the difference**
   What saving your version would change in the file as it is now.
**Take the file's**
   Drop your edits and show the file as it is on disk.
**Keep mine**
   Save your version over the file on disk.

Save never overwrites a file that changed since the tab opened it without
asking.
cards.heading: When the file changes on disk

cards.text:
Building the editor's CodeMirror
--------------------------------

The code editor inside a card is CodeMirror, built into one file that is
checked in (``automationv3/web/static/js/codemirror.bundle.js``), so
running the app needs no Node. To change what it includes, edit
``frontend/codemirror.js`` and rebuild:

.. code-block:: console

   $ cd frontend
   $ npm install
   $ npm run build
cards.heading: Building the editor's CodeMirror

cards.text:
Operating
=========

.. rst-class:: lead

   Running the server and workers, queuing work into reports, and reading
   the results.
cards.heading: Operating

cards.text:
The pieces ---------- .. mermaid:: :caption: The server keeps the queue and the results; workers next to the hardware pull jobs and send results back flowchart TB people([People, in a browser]):::ghost git([The scripts' git repository]):::ghost subgraph server [Server] web[Web app] api[Job API]:::accent queue[("Job queue
sqlite")] workspace[("Workspace
git checkout")] reports[("reports/
run folders")] end subgraph lab [Lab PC] worker[Worker]:::accent sim[sim environment] bench[bench environment] uut[UUTs] end people --> web git -. checked out as .-> workspace web -- renders and lints --> workspace web -- queues --> queue web -- shows --> reports worker -- "checks in, polls, claims
(connects out)" --> api worker -- "streams events, files
and the outcome" --> api api --> queue api -- writes --> reports worker -- hosts --> sim worker -- hosts --> bench sim -- runs --> uut bench -- runs --> uut The server Serves the web app and the job API. It reads scripts from the workspace, keeps the job queue in a sqlite database, and stores finished runs as files under the reports folder. Workers Run next to the hardware, poll the server for jobs they can run, and stream each run's events and attached files back. A server can also run a worker in-process (``--local-worker``). The client Runs on each person's machine against their own worktrees, for a team's central server. It reads requirements from the server and sends it scratch runs and local builds. :doc:`deployment` shows how the pieces fit for a team: the central server, the client and the single-user server.
cards.heading: The pieces

cards.text:
In this section
---------------

:doc:`deployment`
   The central server, the client on each person's machine and the
   single-user server; settings, and mirroring the team's git remote.

:doc:`accounts`
   Single-user and central servers, signing in by emailed link, devices
   and admins.

:doc:`local-client`
   Signing your machine in, and trying scripts from your worktree before
   they're pushed.

:doc:`workers`
   Configuring workers and environments, and how jobs are scheduled.

:doc:`reports`
   Creating reports, adding requirements and tests to them, and reading the
   rollup and runs.

:doc:`configuration-management`
   What a run records, identity, reruns and drift.

:doc:`editor`
   Opening files in tabs and editing scripts a part at a time.

:doc:`scratch`
   Running scripts under development, outside any report.
cards.heading: In this section

cards.text:
Storage
-------

The database holds the job queue and in-progress state, the requirements,
and on a central server the accounts. It is created, or brought up to date,
when the server starts.

Finished runs are plain files under ``--reports-path`` (default
``./reports``):

.. code-block:: text

   reports/
     <report uuid7>/
       report.json            name, UUT versions, scripts, tracked requirements, additions
       runs/
         <run uuid7>/
           run.json           outcome, environment, variation, versions, fingerprint, identity
           events.jsonl       every step, call and phase event, in order
           closure/           the exact files that ran
           files/             files blocks attached
     scratch/                 scratch runs (no report.json)

Being plain files, reports can be archived, copied or inspected with ordinary
tools.
cards.heading: Storage

cards.text:
The local client
================

.. rst-class:: lead

   Write scripts in your own git worktrees and try them as you go, on the
   central server's benches or on your own machine, before anything is
   pushed.
cards.heading: The local client

cards.text:
Signing in
----------

.. code-block:: console

   $ automation-v3 login --server https://automation.example.com
   Your work email: ann@example.com
   We emailed ann@example.com a link. Open it and approve ann-laptop (it works for 15 minutes).
   Signed in to https://automation.example.com as ann@example.com

Open the link and press **Approve**. The client keeps a token for this machine
in ``~/.config/automation-v3/credentials.json``, which only you can read
(``$AUTOMATION_CONFIG_HOME`` or ``$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`` move it). The token acts
as you until you sign out or remove the device on your Account page (see
:doc:`accounts`).

``automation-v3 whoami`` says who this machine is signed in as.
``automation-v3 logout`` signs it out and revokes its token. Commands talk to
the server you last signed in to unless you name another with ``--server``.
cards.heading: Signing in

cards.text:
The local web UI
----------------

.. code-block:: console

   $ automation-v3 client --workspace-path ~/work/scripts
      Signed in to https://automation.example.com as ann@example.com
      Client started: http://localhost:8080/

``client`` serves the workspace pages for your own clone and its worktrees, on
this machine only (it listens on 127.0.0.1). Scripts are rendered and checked
as you save them, with in-work edits marked just as on a single-user server.

What belongs to the team stays on the central server:

- **Requirements**, **Queue**, **Reports** and **Workers** in the header open
  the central server's pages.
- ``:req:`` references show the central server's text for the requirements
  your workspace verifies (its ``automation.json``). They're looked up live
  and kept for a minute.
- **Run in scratch** uploads the script's files, edits included, to the
  central server's scratch space and opens the run there. Start the client
  with ``--config worker.json`` and you can pick **on this machine** instead.
  The run then happens in the client's own worker, with the environments
  that config hosts, and its results stay in the client's folder
  (``~/.local/share/automation-v3/client``, or ``--data-path``). The client's
  **Scratch** page lists those runs.
- **Queue on the central server…** opens the central server's queue dialog
  for your branch. Reports run what was pushed, so push first.

On the central server, **Run again** on an uploaded run runs the same files
again, since the worktree they came from is on someone else's machine.
Upload again from the client to run your latest edits.
cards.heading: The local web UI

cards.text:
Local builds
------------

To run a scratch test on a build you've just made, tell the client where each
UUT's builds land on your machine, in ``client.json`` next to your
credentials:

.. code-block:: json

   {"builds": {"demo": "~/work/demo/build/out"}}

For each UUT a script uses, **Run in scratch** then offers a version:

- **upload your local build**, when the newest build in that folder isn't in
  the build repository yet. A **New local build** badge marks it. Choosing it
  pushes the build to the build repository, using your own credentials (the
  UUT's plugin does the pushing; the central server never handles builds),
  and runs on it.
- the build repository's versions, newest first, with your uploaded build
  marked **your local build**, and the one you used last marked
  **last used**.

The default is your local build once it's uploaded, then whatever you used
last, then the newest version. Uploaded builds are cleaned up by the build
repository's own rules, and they're for scratch only: reports offer and
accept only the versions the UUT's plugin releases (its ``report_versions``,
see :doc:`../blocks/uuts-and-environments`).

From the command line, ``automation-v3 builds`` lists your local builds and
whether each is uploaded, and ``automation-v3 scratch SCRIPT --uut demo=local``
uses yours, uploading it first if needed.
cards.heading: Local builds

cards.text:
Trying a script from the command line
-------------------------------------

.. code-block:: console

   $ cd ~/work/scripts/rvts
   $ automation-v3 scratch BRA/tc_bra_00004.rst
   Queued BRA/tc_bra_00004.rst (sim): https://automation.example.com/reports/scratch/runs/0193...

   BRA/tc_bra_00004.rst (sim), scratch mode
     ok   step 1
     FAIL step 2
     ...
     fail     BRA/tc_bra_00004.rst (sim)

``scratch`` reads the script, and every ``core.rst`` and import it loads, from
your worktree as they are on disk, uncommitted edits included. It checks them
first and stops on any error. Then it uploads them to the central server's
scratch space, where they run on its workers. It prints each step as it runs
and exits non-zero unless every run passed.

``--env`` and ``--variation`` (both repeatable) narrow what runs, and
``--uut NAME=VERSION`` picks UUT versions (the newest by default).
``--no-wait`` queues the runs and prints their links without waiting.

Uploaded files only ever run in scratch. Each upload is recorded as
**uploaded**, with the branch your worktree has checked out and the machine
that sent it, and never counts toward a report. To put a script in a report,
push it, then queue it on the central server, which runs what was pushed (see
:doc:`deployment`).

To run on your own machine instead, with no server at all, use
``automation-v3 run`` (see :doc:`scratch`). Its results stay on your machine.
cards.heading: Trying a script from the command line

cards.text:
Reports
=======

.. rst-class:: lead

   A report is a named body of evidence: runs against chosen UUT versions,
   rolled up to the requirements they verify. It grows as you add to it.
cards.heading: Reports

cards.text:
Creating a report
-----------------

**Reports → New report** asks for:

- a **name**, e.g. "Brakes, release 1.1 candidate";
- the **workspace** its scripts come from.

The report starts empty. Its UUT versions come from the first tests added
to it (see `UUT versions`_).
cards.heading: Creating a report

cards.text:
Who can change a report
-----------------------

On a central server (see :doc:`accounts`) a report belongs to whoever made
it: its **owner**. The owner can add **collaborators** by email in the
report's **History → People** section, and remove them again. Collaborators
don't need to have signed in yet.

Everyone signed in can read every report. Only its owner, its collaborators
and admins can change it: add to it, rerun its runs, change its versions,
edit and rename its document, and freeze or reopen it. Anyone else sees
**View only** in its header and none of those buttons; the document's
source opens read-only. A report made before the server had accounts
has no owner, so only admins can change it.

**Reports** lists the reports you own or collaborate on. **Everyone** shows
the whole team's, with each one's owner. Each addition and run records who
queued it.

On a single-user server there are no owners, and anyone can change anything.
cards.heading: Who can change a report

cards.text:
Adding to a report ------------------ **Add requirements…** Adds every script linked to the chosen requirements, and **tracks** the requirements: they appear in the report's rollup. **Add a test…** Adds one script, without tracking its requirements. Each addition queues every combination of the script's environments and variations (you can narrow both), on the report's UUT versions. Combinations that have already passed on the report's versions are left out of an addition, unless you tick **Run again what already passed**. .. mermaid:: :caption: What an addition queues flowchart TB add["Add requirements…
or Add a test…"] --> scripts["The scripts
(linked to the requirements)"] scripts --> combos["Each script's environments
× variations, as narrowed"] combos --> passed{{"Already passed on
the report's versions?"}} passed -- "yes, unless Run again" --> left[Left out]:::ghost passed -- no --> jobs["Queued, one job each,
on the report's UUT versions"]:::accent
cards.heading: Adding to a report

cards.text:
UUT versions
~~~~~~~~~~~~

A report tests one version of each UUT its scripts use, and those versions
are the only ones that count:

- The first addition that needs a UUT sets the report's version for it: the
  queue dialog offers a version (the newest by default) only for a UUT the
  report has none for yet. Later additions run on the report's versions.
- **Versions…**, beside the versions in the report's header, changes them.
  It shows how many combinations the change leaves outdated, and queues
  nothing. It waits while runs are in progress, and a frozen report keeps
  its versions.
- A combination whose latest run used another version is **outdated**:
  amber, e.g. *Passed on vm 3.1.0*, never green. Its requirement can't be
  green until it is brought up to date. The header counts them.
- To bring them up to date, use **Update tests…** (it offers everything that
  hasn't passed on the report's versions) or a run's **Rerun on vm 3.2.0**,
  which runs the same script again on the report's versions.

The header lists only the UUTs the report's runs use.

The Requirements page and the script view also have an **Add to** / **Queue
in** report picker. Leaving it blank creates a new report in one step, named
after what it covers.
cards.heading: UUT versions

cards.text:
Tracking requirements before their tests exist
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

A report can follow the development of a whole subsystem, or any set of
requirements, from before any script is written. On the Requirements page,
pick a subsystem and tick **Select all in** it (or pick requirements one by
one: those no script references yet can be picked too). If nothing can run
yet, the dialog offers to **track** them instead: the report lists them as
*no tests*, which is neither green nor red.

As scripts are written, **Update tests…** on the report checks every tracked
requirement against the workspace again, with every test added on its own,
and runs what it finds, leaving out what already passed on the report's
versions.
cards.heading: Tracking requirements before their tests exist

cards.text:
The rollup ---------- Each tracked requirement is judged on the latest run of every combination of every script linked to it: .. list-table:: :header-rows: 1 :widths: 20 80 * - State - When * - green - the latest run of every linked combination passed * - red - the latest run of any linked combination failed * - partial - anything else: not run yet, queued, running, blocked or error * - no tests - no script references it yet A combination whose latest run used other UUT versions than the report's counts as outdated, which is never green (see `UUT versions`_). .. mermaid:: :caption: How a tracked requirement is judged flowchart TB req([A tracked requirement]) --> linked{{"Does any script
reference it?"}} linked -- no --> none[no tests]:::ghost linked -- yes --> latest["The latest run of every combination
of every linked script"] latest --> failed{{"Any failed, on the
report's versions?"}} failed -- yes --> red[red]:::danger failed -- no --> all{{All passed, on them?}} all -- yes --> green[green]:::success all -- no --> partial["partial: not run, queued, running,
blocked, error, incomplete or outdated"]:::warning Linked scripts that weren't added, and variations that were left out, count as not run, so a requirement is only green when its whole coverage passed.
cards.heading: The rollup

cards.text:
Reading a report
----------------

A report's pages share a navigation column on the left:

**Document**
   The report's document, ``report.rst``, shown with the report's data as it
   is now: by default its identification, summary, open issues (each
   combination whose latest run didn't pass, and why), every tracked
   requirement with the combinations covering it, the results, reruns and
   failures. While runs are in progress each part refreshes itself.
   **Edit document…** opens its source beside a live preview: write what the
   report is for in prose, and move, filter or drop the parts (see
   :doc:`../reference/report-documents`). Below it are the fields of the
   exported PDF.

   In the navigation, Document opens into a tree of subsystems, their
   requirements, and the tests run for each, by their titles. A subsystem or
   requirement shows the document narrowed to that subsystem; a test opens
   its latest run. Scripts added on their own, without a requirement, are
   under **Other tests**. Each entry has a dot for how it stands:

   .. list-table::
      :widths: 20 80

      * - green
        - passed
      * - red
        - failed, or ended in an error
      * - amber
        - partial: incomplete, steps to be written, blocked, or outdated
          (ran on another UUT version than the report's)
      * - hollow
        - not run yet, or no tests yet
      * - pulsing
        - running

   A subsystem or requirement also shows how many of its entries have
   issues. Branches with issues start open; **Issues only** hides the rest.
   The navigation remembers what you open and close.

   Clicking a subsystem shows only its requirements; a requirement also
   scrolls to it, and a test to its rows. The address follows, e.g.
   ``/reports/<id>/runs?subsystem=EPS#req-VM-EPS-002``, so it can be shared,
   and back and forward work.

**Values touched**
   The values the latest runs read, set or fixed through connectors, grouped
   by connector (e.g. ``vm.eps``), with every fixed value listed first.

**History**
   What was added to the report, every combination's latest and earlier
   runs, and scripts that couldn't be added.

While runs are in progress, the page and its navigation refresh every few
seconds. Rename a report with the pencil beside its title; its name is the
title of its exported document too.
cards.heading: Reading a report

cards.text:
Reading a run
-------------

A run page is the script's own document (as the workspace shows it) with what
came of each step after it, for the variation it ran:

- under the breadcrumbs, the variation, the outcome and the **Rerun**
  button;
- **Details**: the environment, UUT versions, mode, timings and
  configuration facts (see :doc:`configuration-management`);
- each step with its badge, its duration to the millisecond, its output,
  the block calls made in it, attached files, and, if it failed, the message
  and the code it failed at;
- preconditions collapsed to their description and badge, expanding to each
  phase.

Earlier runs of the same combination are kept and listed with the latest.
cards.heading: Reading a run

cards.text:
Issuing a report
----------------

When a report has to be handed over as a formal document, **Freeze** it.
Freezing needs every run to have finished. The report takes no more runs, and
its site and PDF are built with Sphinx in the background; the report's page
says so while they build, and then opens the site. A frozen report *is* its
site: the document as it was frozen and a page per run, served with a bar
for its actions:

**PDF**
   The document: a title page, contents, a signature page, the applicable and
   reference documents, then the report's document, with each failing run's
   document as an appendix.

**Bundle**
   Writes and downloads ``report-<id>.zip``:

   ``report-<id>/``
      The report folder as it is kept: ``report.json``, the document's source
      ``report.rst`` and its ``template/``, and for each run the files it
      executed, every event it recorded and the files attached to it.

   ``MANIFEST.sha256``
      A SHA-256 for every file in the report folder. The PDF prints the
      manifest's own SHA-256, on its title page and under Identification, so
      anyone can check the bundle is the one the document describes.

   ``report.pdf``, ``report.tex``
      The PDF, and the LaTeX it was made from.

   ``site/``
      The static site: open ``site/index.html`` in a browser, no server needed.

**Reopen**
   Takes runs again, and drops the site and PDF: they no longer describe the
   report until it is frozen again.

If the build fails (a broken template, say), the report stays frozen and its
page shows why and the build's log, with **Rebuild**.

Before exporting, fill in the document's fields (on the Document page, under
**Document fields**, **Edit…**): its number, revision and author, who signs for each role
on the signature page, and its applicable and reference documents, one per
line as ``NUMBER | REVISION | TITLE``. Requirement texts are copied into the
report when requirements are added, so the PDF quotes what was tested
against. The document's title is the report's name.

.. mermaid::
   :caption: A report takes runs until it is frozen, and again once reopened

   stateDiagram-v2
     [*] --> open: New report
     open --> frozen: Freeze, every run finished
     frozen --> open: Reopen
     open: Open, takes additions and reruns
     frozen: Frozen, its site and PDF built, exported as report-ID.zip

A frozen report can't be picked as a target, and **Rerun** is gone from its
runs. Only whether a report is frozen is kept, not a history of freezes, so
the manifest's SHA-256 is what tells two exports apart.

The same works without the server, on a report folder:

.. code-block:: console

   $ automation-v3 report edit reports/<id> --title "Brakes qualification" \
         --number TR-0042 --revision A --author "J. Smith" \
         --sign "Approved by=J. Doe" --applicable "SRS-1 | C | Requirements"
   $ automation-v3 report export reports/<id> --out issued/
   $ automation-v3 report reopen reports/<id>

``report export`` freezes, builds (waiting for it) and writes the bundle.
Building needs Sphinx, and the PDF a TeX distribution with ``latexmk`` (e.g.
TeX Live), on the server's host.
cards.heading: Issuing a report

cards.text:
The document template
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

A workspace keeps its template in a ``report/`` folder beside its ``rvts/``
folder; without one, a built-in placeholder template (a made-up company) is
used. Start from the built-in one, in
``automationv3/services/reports/template/``:

``template.json``
   The company name, the marking printed in every footer, the document type
   on the title page, and the signature page's roles.

``latex.tex_t``
   The PDF's LaTeX: Sphinx's LaTeX template (written with ``<%= value %>`` and
   ``<% statement %>``), with the title page, headers and footers, signature
   page and documents table, and how the document's marked parts look. The
   report's values are ``automation.title``, ``automation.number`` and so on
   (see the built-in one).

``report.rst``
   The document a new report starts from: prose, and directives where the
   report's data goes (see :doc:`../reference/report-documents`).

``snippets/`` (optional)
   Snippets overriding the built-in ones, to change how a directive writes
   its part of the document.

``logo.pdf``, and any other file ``latex.tex_t`` includes.

A report copies its workspace's template when it is created (the built-in
one if the workspace has none), so a report's look never changes under it.
Its document, ``report.rst``, is the report's own from then on.

Verdicts and requirement texts carry a class, so every output can style
them: a verdict is ``:verdict:`fail``` (the class ``verdict-fail``), and a
requirement's text a ``.. container:: requirement``. In the PDF these are
``\DUrole{verdict-fail}{...}`` and ``\begin{sphinxuseclass}{requirement}``,
which use ``\DUroleverdict-fail`` or the ``sphinxclassrequirement``
environment when ``latex.tex_t`` defines them, and leave the text as it is
when it doesn't. The built-in template colors the verdicts and sets
requirements in italics; pages and the site style them with CSS.
cards.heading: The document template

cards.text:
Requirements in practice
========================

.. rst-class:: lead

   Importing specs from DOORS on a schedule, reading them and what changed,
   and keeping scripts honest when a requirement moves under them.
cards.heading: Requirements in practice

cards.text:
How specs get in
----------------

The DOORS exporter writes an export folder (see
:doc:`../reference/requirements-export`); ``automation-v3 requirements
import`` reads it into the server's database. Run both from a scheduled CI
job, on a runner that can reach DOORS and the server's database:

.. code-block:: yaml

   # .gitlab-ci.yml
   import-requirements:
     tags: [automation-server]     # a shell runner on the server's host
     rules:
       - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"
     script:
       - doors-export --out "export-$CI_PIPELINE_ID"
       - automation-v3 requirements import "export-$CI_PIPELINE_ID"
           --dbpath /srv/automation/automationv3.db
     artifacts:
       paths: ["export-$CI_PIPELINE_ID/"]
       expire_in: 90 days

The import is safe to run as often as you like:

- **Unchanged content changes nothing.** The import is logged as having
  looked, and the log of changes only grows when DOORS did.
- **Trunk only moves forward.** An export older than the trunk already
  imported (by its ``exported_at``) is refused, so a re-run of an old
  pipeline can't roll trunk back. Re-running the *same* export is fine.
- **A baseline never changes.** Exporting a baseline again with different
  content fails the job, which is what you want to hear about.
- **All or nothing.** An export with any problem (an attribute not in its
  schema, an id in two specs, a baseline set naming a baseline that doesn't
  exist) is refused whole, and the job fails with every problem listed.

Keeping each pipeline's export folder as an artifact means any import can be
looked at, or run again, later.
cards.heading: How specs get in

cards.text:
From a spreadsheet or a list
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Without DOORS, keep each spec as a spreadsheet (Excel, or CSV) or a text
file, one requirement per line (see :ref:`flat-requirements`).

On the **Imports** page, upload the file. A page follows that asks which
spec it is and shows each column with a few of its values and a guessed role:
id, text, satisfies, section, an attribute (with its name), or ignored.
**Preview** shows what importing would do against what is there now: the
requirements added, removed and changed, with each change word by word, or
every problem in the file with its row. Nothing changes until **Import**.
Uploading a file of the same name again, next month's export say, fills
everything in as it was read last time, columns matched by their headers even
if they moved.

On the command line, name the spec; the columns are guessed from the
headers:

.. code-block:: bash

   automation-v3 requirements import srs.csv --spec SRS --title "VM SRS" --parents SYS
   automation-v3 requirements import srs.csv --spec SRS --baseline 1.0
   automation-v3 requirements import vm.xlsx --spec SRS-VM --sheet Requirements

Import the file again whenever it changes: what changed shows as it would
from DOORS, and scripts referencing a changed requirement become suspect.
Even with no requirements imported at all, scripts' ``:req:`` references
still list each id with the scripts that test it, and reports still roll up
by requirement; only the text, its history and suspects need an import.
cards.heading: From a spreadsheet or a list

cards.text:
Where requirements live
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Requirements live in one server's database, and everything reads them from
there:

- **On its own** (``automation-v3 server``, no settings): this machine's
  database. Import on the command line with ``--dbpath``, or on the
  **Imports** page, where anyone can upload.
- **A central server**: its database. Admins import on the Imports page or
  with ``--server URL`` from a signed-in machine.
- **The local client** (``automation-v3 client``) keeps none of its own: its
  ``:req:`` references show the central server's text, and its Requirements
  pages are the central server's.
cards.heading: Where requirements live

cards.text:
On a central server
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

A central server (see :doc:`deployment`) takes imports from admins only, two
ways:

- **Requirements → Imports** has an upload form for admins: a zip of the
  export folder, with ``manifest.json`` at its top or in its one top folder,
  or a spreadsheet or list, matched and previewed as above.
- ``automation-v3 requirements import SOURCE --server URL``, from a machine
  signed in as an admin (see :doc:`local-client`), uploads each folder
  (zipped) or file. A CI job can do the same with its own admin's device, with no
  access to the server's database needed.

Either way the import is recorded with who made it, shown on the Imports
page. The same rules apply: unchanged content changes nothing, trunk only
moves forward, and a bad export is refused whole.
cards.heading: On a central server

cards.text:
The Requirements pages
----------------------

**Requirements**
   The requirements in a context (trunk, a baseline set or one spec's
   baseline), by spec or subsystem, with the scripts that test each. Pick
   requirements to queue their scripts. A spec can be read as the document it
   is, with its headings, prose and figures, and its requirements linked.

**A requirement**
   Its text and attributes, what it satisfies and what satisfies it, the
   scripts that test it, and its history: each trunk import that changed it,
   word by word, and the baselines it is in.

**Changes**
   What was added, removed and changed between any two contexts, for
   everything, one spec or one subsystem: Release 1 against trunk, or trunk
   as of one import against trunk as of another.

**Suspects**
   Links that may need another look (below).

**Imports**
   Each import, newest first, and what it changed in trunk.
cards.heading: The Requirements pages

cards.text:
Which requirements a workspace verifies
---------------------------------------

A workspace verifies trunk unless it says otherwise. A release branch names
the baseline set it verifies in ``automation.json`` at its root:

.. code-block:: json

   {"requirements": "set:Release 1"}

Its Requirements pages, suspects and new reports then use that context, and
the setting travels with the branch. Any page can still show another context
for a moment with the picker in its side column.
cards.heading: Which requirements a workspace verifies

cards.text:
Suspect links
-------------

When a requirement's text changes, whatever was written against the old text
may be wrong. Two kinds of link become **suspect**:

- a script's ``:req:`` reference, when the requirement's text in the
  workspace's context changed since the script was last reviewed;
- a requirement's ``:satisfies:`` link, when its parent's text changed in
  trunk since the link was last reviewed.

A link counts as reviewed against the text it first meets, so only later
changes make it suspect, and only changes to the *text*: a new attribute
value or a reformatted export doesn't. The Suspects page shows each one with
what changed since its review; fix the script or requirement if it needs it,
then **Mark reviewed**. On a central server the review records who marked it.
cards.heading: Suspect links

cards.text:
What a report records
---------------------

A report verifies requirements in its workspace's context, and records it.
For each requirement it tracks, it keeps the text and the version (the spec
and a hash of the text) it took on, and each run keeps the version of every
requirement its script covers. When a requirement's text changes after the
report took it on, the report's document says so beside it: a pass against
the old text is still a pass against the old text.
cards.heading: What a report records

cards.text:
The scratch space
=================

.. rst-class:: lead

   Run scripts while you write them, without adding anything to a report.
cards.heading: The scratch space

cards.text:
In work and checked in
----------------------

The workspace shows each branch's files as they are on disk. When a script,
or a ``core.rst`` or import it loads, has edits that aren't committed, its
page says so and offers three views:

**In work**
   The files as they are on disk, edits included.
**Checked in**
   The files as committed on the branch.
**Changes**
   What the edits change, file by file.

Reports run only what is checked in: **Queue…** builds from the committed
files, says which scripts have edits it is leaving out, and won't take a
script that isn't committed at all. Scratch is where in-work files run.
cards.heading: In work and checked in

cards.text:
Running in scratch
------------------

**Run in scratch** on a script's page runs it outside any report: the
variation picked on the page (or every variation), in the environment picked
beside the button (or every environment it supports), with the newest UUT
versions. It runs the files you're looking at: in work, or as checked in.

**Scratch** in the navigation lists the runs, newest first, with the files
each used and a link back to its script. **Run again** re-reads the same
files as they are now (in work or checked in, as before), so the loop is:
edit, Run again, read the result. **Clear finished runs** deletes the
finished ones.
cards.heading: Running in scratch

cards.text:
How it differs from a report
----------------------------

- Scratch runs may use files that were never committed.
- They never appear in a report or a rollup.
- There is one scratch space. On a central server each run belongs to
  whoever ran it: **Scratch** shows your runs (**Everyone** shows the
  team's), and **Clear my finished runs** clears only yours.
- On the queue, scratch runs go ahead of reports' runs, so the edit, run,
  read loop stays quick while a long report is queued (see :doc:`workers`).
cards.heading: How it differs from a report

cards.text:
When the script works
---------------------

A scratch run can't be promoted into a report, because it may have run text
that was never committed. Commit the script, then use **Queue in a report…**
on the scratch run's page to run it properly.
cards.heading: When the script works

cards.text:
From the command line
---------------------

``automation-v3 run`` is the offline equivalent: it runs scripts on your
machine with no server, prints each step and writes a report folder locally.
See :doc:`../reference/cli`.
cards.heading: From the command line

cards.text:
Workers
=======

.. rst-class:: lead

   A worker hosts environments, pulls jobs it can run, and reports back. Put
   one on every machine that can reach a simulator or bench.
cards.heading: Workers

cards.text:
Starting a worker
-----------------

.. code-block:: bash

   automation-v3 worker --central-server automation.example:8080 --config worker.json

The worker connects out to the server, so lab machines need no inbound
access. By default it also serves a small status page on ``--port``; add
``--no-http`` to run without it.
cards.heading: Starting a worker
The config file

cards.text:
Worker tokens
-------------

A central server (see :doc:`accounts`) only takes work from workers with a
**worker token**. An admin makes one on the **Admin** page, one per worker or
bench, and it is shown once. Give it to the worker in its config, or in
``AUTOMATION_WORKER_TOKEN`` (which wins):

.. code-block:: json

   {
     "token": "av3w_...",
     "environments": {"sim": {}}
   }

The token is sent with every call to the job API. A worker's address belongs
to the token it first checked in with, so another token can't take over its
jobs. Each run records the name of the token whose worker ran it, and the
Workers page shows it. **Revoke** stops that worker at once: its next call
is refused, and the jobs it held become errors once it goes quiet, as for
any missing worker.

A single-user server needs no token, and ignores one.
cards.heading: Worker tokens

cards.text:
What a worker offers
--------------------

When it checks in, a worker tells the server which environments it hosts and
each one's fingerprint. The server only hands it jobs for those environments,
and a pinned rerun only to a worker whose fingerprint matches.
cards.heading: What a worker offers

cards.text:
Scheduling ---------- Pending jobs are offered to workers **scratch runs first**, then reports' runs, each oldest first. Scratch runs are short and someone is waiting on them, so a long report queued ahead doesn't hold up the edit, run, read loop. Reports' runs stay first in, first out. Workers schedule **warm-first**: 1. Every pending job the worker can run is **probed** against the environment as it is: if its UUT versions are already installed, its preconditions are checked and healed. 2. The first job whose preconditions hold runs. Others are released back to the queue untouched. 3. If none does, the first in the queue's order runs in **force mode**: UUT versions are installed if needed and started fresh, then the job's preconditions run. A precondition that still fails makes the run :status:`blocked`. .. mermaid:: :caption: Warm-first: run what fits the environment as it is, and only start fresh when nothing does flowchart TB idle([Poll for pending jobs]) --> next{{"Another pending job
it can run?"}} next -- yes --> installed{{"Probe it: its UUT versions
already installed?"}} installed -- yes --> holds{{"Its preconditions
hold, or heal?"}} installed -- no --> release[Release it to the queue] holds -- no --> release release --> next holds -- yes --> run[Run its steps]:::success next -- none left --> any{{Any pending job at all?}} any -- no --> idle any -- yes --> force["Force mode, the oldest:
install if needed, start fresh"]:::warning force --> holds2{{"Its preconditions
hold, or heal?"}} holds2 -- yes --> run holds2 -- no --> blocked[blocked]:::warning UUTs are never torn down between jobs. The run page records the mode a run ran in, and for each UUT whether it was installed or kept.
cards.heading: Scheduling

cards.text:
Talking to the server
---------------------

A worker only ever makes requests to the server, under ``/runner``:

.. mermaid::
   :caption: One job, from the worker's poll to its outcome in the report

   sequenceDiagram
     participant W as Worker
     participant S as Server
     participant R as reports/
     W->>S: POST /workers: check in, with environments and fingerprints
     loop every 2 s while idle
       W->>S: GET /jobs?worker_url=…
       S-->>W: pending jobs it can run, oldest first
     end
     W->>S: POST /jobs/ID/claim
     S-->>W: the job, with its closure
     W->>S: POST /jobs/ID/start
     alt a probe that doesn't fit
       W->>S: POST /jobs/ID/release
       Note over S: pending again, for any worker
     else it runs
       loop as the script runs
         W->>S: POST /jobs/ID/events, /files
         S->>R: events.jsonl, files/
       end
       W->>S: POST /jobs/ID/complete: outcome, installed, fingerprint, mode
       S->>R: run.json
       Note over S: the job leaves the queue
     end

A worker checks in again every minute. One that hasn't for five minutes is
taken as lost, and the jobs it held end in :status:`error`.

.. mermaid::
   :caption: A job in the queue. Its outcome is kept in the run's run.json, not in the queue

   stateDiagram-v2
     [*] --> pending: queued
     pending --> claimed: claim
     claimed --> running: start
     claimed --> pending: release
     running --> pending: release
     running --> finished: complete
     claimed --> finished: worker lost
     running --> finished: worker lost
     finished --> [*]
cards.heading: Talking to the server

cards.text:
Outcomes
--------

:status:`passed`
   Every step passed.

:status:`failed`
   A step failed; the rest didn't run.

:status:`blocked`
   A precondition couldn't be established, so the test didn't run.

:status:`error`
   Something outside the script went wrong: an install failed, the worker
   raised. The run page shows the traceback.
cards.heading: Outcomes

cards.text:
Running the server with a worker
--------------------------------

For a single machine:

.. code-block:: bash

   automation-v3 server --workspace-path ./scripts --local-worker --config worker.json

The in-process worker takes jobs straight from the server's database. Other
workers can still connect.
cards.heading: Running the server with a worker

cards.text:
Concepts ======== .. rst-class:: lead The vocabulary used throughout these docs and the web app. .. mermaid:: :caption: A script, the jobs it is queued as, where they run, and what their results count towards flowchart TB script[Script] closure["core.rst chain + imports
(the closure)"] combos["environments × variations × UUT versions"] job[Job] worker[Worker] env[Environment] uut[UUT] run[Run] report[Report] req[Requirement]:::accent script -- loads --> closure script -- declares --> combos script -. references .-> req combos -- queued as, one each --> job job -- pulled by --> worker worker -- hosts --> env env -- runs --> uut job -- recorded as --> run run -- collected in --> report report -- rolls up to --> req
cards.heading: Concepts

cards.text:
Scripts and their closure
-------------------------

Script
   An ``.rst`` document containing at least one ``rvt`` block. Each form in an
   ``rvt`` block is a step, a definition or a directive. See
   :doc:`../scripts/first-script`.

``core.rst``
   A folder's shared definitions. A script loads the ``core.rst`` of every
   folder from the workspace root down to its own, then those of folders it
   imports with ``(import FOLDER)``.

Closure
   The script plus every file it loaded. The closure is hashed, and copied
   into the run, so a result can always be traced to the exact text that ran.

Workspace
   A git checkout (or worktree) the app reads scripts from. The app never
   writes to it.
cards.heading: Scripts and their closure

cards.text:
What a script runs against
--------------------------

UUT
   A unit under test, e.g. a controller's software. A UUT type is a Python
   plugin that lists its versions, installs one into an environment, starts
   it, and gives scripts a **handle** to talk to it. Scripts declare what
   they test with ``(uut :demo)``.

Environment
   Where a script runs: a simulator, a bench, a rig. Hosted by workers.
   Scripts declare where they can run with ``(environments :sim :bench)``.

Variation
   One way of running a script, binding the same symbols to different values,
   e.g. ``normal`` and ``limp-home`` braking modes. A script with three
   variations that runs in two environments has six **combinations**.

Precondition
   The state a script needs before its steps, with an optional **heal** that
   establishes it. Workers use preconditions to schedule work on warm hardware.
cards.heading: What a script runs against

cards.text:
Running
-------

Job
   One combination of a script queued to run: script, environment, variation
   and UUT versions.

Worker
   A process next to the hardware that hosts one or more environments, pulls
   jobs it can run, executes them and streams results back.

Run
   The record of one executed job: its outcome (:status:`passed`,
   :status:`failed`, :status:`blocked` or :status:`error`), the events of
   each step, files blocks attached, and the closure.

Report
   A named collection of runs against chosen UUT versions, that grows as
   requirements and tests are added to it. Its **rollup** shows each tracked
   requirement as green, red or partial.

Identity
   The hash of a run's closure, variation values, UUT versions and the
   environment's fingerprint. Two runs with the same identity ran the same
   test on the same configuration.
cards.heading: Running

cards.text:
Who does what
-------------

Script writer
   Writes scripts in rst and edn, using definitions and BuildingBlocks.
   Start at :doc:`../scripts/index`.

Block developer
   Writes BuildingBlocks, UUTs and environments in Python.
   Start at :doc:`../blocks/index`.

Operator
   Runs the server and workers, queues reports and reads their results.
   Start at :doc:`../operating/index`.
cards.heading: Who does what

cards.text:
Getting started
===============

.. rst-class:: lead

   Run the sample test set on one machine: a server, a worker, the simulated
   ``demo`` UUT and a dozen example scripts.
cards.heading: Getting started

cards.text:
The demo
--------

From a clone of the repository, with Python 3.10 or newer:

.. code-block:: bash

   python -m venv .venv
   source .venv/bin/activate
   pip install -e ".[docs]"
   automation-v3 demo

Open http://localhost:8080.

``demo`` builds a fresh ``./demo`` folder and serves it with a worker in the
same process. It holds a workspace (a git repository of the sample scripts,
with three more branches), the sample requirements, the ``sim`` and ``bench``
environments' work directories, and these docs, linked as **Docs** in the
app's navigation. Running it again deletes the earlier demo and starts over;
it never deletes a folder it didn't make.

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 30 70

   * - Option
     - Meaning
   * - ``--path PATH``
     - the demo's folder (default ``./demo``)
   * - ``--port PORT``
     - the port to serve on (default 8080)
   * - ``--no-docs``
     - don't build the documentation

The install must be editable: the demo reads the sample scripts and these
docs' sources from the checkout.
cards.heading: The demo

cards.text:
Setting it up by hand
---------------------

To run against the sample set without the demo, load the sample data and
start a server and a worker:

.. code-block:: bash

   python test/data/load_sample.py
   python test/data/make_workspaces.py
   automation-v3 server --workspace-path ./test/data/git_repos/master

In a second terminal:

.. code-block:: bash

   automation-v3 worker --port 8081 --central-server localhost:8080 --config test/data/worker.json

Or run everything in one process, with a worker inside the server:

.. code-block:: bash

   automation-v3 server --workspace-path ./test/data/git_repos/master --local-worker --config test/data/worker.json

Add ``--docs-path docs/_build/html`` to serve a build of these docs at
``/docs``.
cards.heading: Setting it up by hand

cards.text:
A first tour
------------

1. **Workspace** shows the script tree. Open ``BRA/tc_bra_00004.rst``: the
   variation selector under the breadcrumbs switches the page between the
   ``normal``, ``limp-home`` and ``emergency`` variations, and **Details**
   lists where it runs, what it tests and its variations.
2. Press **Queue…** to run it. Leave the defaults and queue: a report is
   created for it.
3. **Reports** lists the report. Open a run to see each step with its badge,
   its duration and anything it printed.
4. **Requirements** lists requirements with their linked scripts. Pick a few
   and add them to a report to see the rollup.

``test/data/rvts/README.rst`` lists what each example script shows; several
fail, block or refuse to queue on purpose.
cards.heading: A first tour

cards.text:
Running without a server
------------------------

``automation-v3 run`` runs scripts on this machine with no server or database,
using the same worker config. It prints each step, writes a normal report
folder and exits non-zero unless every run passed:

.. code-block:: bash

   automation-v3 run BRA/tc_bra_00004.rst --root test/data/rvts --config test/data/worker.json --variation limp-home --uut demo=1.0.0
cards.heading: Running without a server

cards.text:
Building these docs
-------------------

.. code-block:: bash

   cd docs
   make html

The site is written to ``docs/_build/html``.
cards.heading: Building these docs

cards.text:
Motivation
==========

.. rst-class:: lead

   Why automation exists, and the handful of ideas every other part of it
   follows from.

Verification of a vehicle controller (or any embedded unit) produces two
things: evidence that each requirement holds, and the scripts that produced
that evidence. In practice both rot. Scripts become opaque code that only
their author can review; results end up in spreadsheets detached from the
exact software, test code and bench that produced them; and rerunning a test
"the same way" is a matter of hope.

automation is built around a few commitments that address those problems
directly.
cards.heading: Motivation

cards.text:
Scripts are documents
---------------------

A test script is a reStructuredText document. Its prose says what is being
tested and why; its ``rvt`` blocks hold the steps. The web app renders the
script as a readable page, where each BuildingBlock can present its arguments
in the clearest form (a configuration as a table rather than a nested map).

The aim is that a reviewer who has never seen the script language can read a
script and agree it tests what the requirement says. Features such as titled
blocks, ``rvt-variant`` sections and described heals exist to make the
rendered document read well, not just to make the script run.

.. seealso:: :doc:`../scripts/documenting`
cards.heading: Scripts are documents

cards.text:
Requirements are the unit of progress
-------------------------------------

Scripts reference the requirements they verify (``:req:`VMCBRA00001```).
A report rolls every run up to those requirements: a requirement is
:status:`passed` (green) only when every linked script passed in every
environment and variation it should run in, :status:`failed` (red) if any
of them failed, and :status:`partial` otherwise. The question a report
answers is "which requirements are verified?", not "which scripts ran?".
cards.heading: Requirements are the unit of progress

cards.text:
A result is only as good as its configuration
---------------------------------------------

Every run records exactly what produced it:

- the **closure**: the script and every ``core.rst`` and import it loaded,
  stored with the run;
- the **variation** values it ran with;
- the **UUT versions** and the digests of the installed bits;
- the **environment fingerprint**: facts about the simulator or bench, and
  the framework's own version and commit.

These hash to an **identity**. A rerun reproduces the original identity or
says plainly that it did not: if no worker's environment matches any more,
the rerun is refused with a diff of what drifted, and can only be forced as
:status:`not identical`.

.. seealso:: :doc:`../operating/configuration-management`
cards.heading: A result is only as good as its configuration

cards.text:
Workers pull, and keep hardware warm
------------------------------------

Benches are scarce and slow to set up. Workers live next to the hardware and
pull jobs from the server, so a lab machine needs no inbound access. They
prefer the job whose **preconditions** already hold (or can be healed) in the
environment as it is, and only reinstall and restart UUTs fresh when nothing
queued fits. Scripts say what state they need instead of always starting from
scratch, and the scheduler takes advantage of it.

.. seealso:: :doc:`../scripts/preconditions`, :doc:`../operating/workers`
cards.heading: Workers pull, and keep hardware warm

cards.text:
A small language, extended in Python
------------------------------------

Script code is a small Lisp written in `edn <https://github.com/edn-format/edn>`_.
It is deliberately limited: definitions, a few special forms, and calls to
**BuildingBlocks**. Anything that touches hardware, needs a library or
deserves careful engineering is a BuildingBlock written in Python by a block
developer, with its own syntax check and rendering. Script writers compose
blocks; block developers make them trustworthy.

.. seealso:: :doc:`../blocks/index`
cards.heading: A small language, extended in Python

cards.text:
Authored in git, edited anywhere
--------------------------------

Scripts live in git and are reviewed like code. The web app's workspace
renders a checkout's scripts, lints them and queues them. On your own
machine it also :doc:`edits them <../operating/editor>`, writing the same
files any other editor would; committing stays with git. While a script is
under development, the :doc:`scratch space <../operating/scratch>` runs it
straight from the working
tree without touching any report.
cards.heading: Authored in git, edited anywhere
