cards.text:
Command line
============

.. rst-class:: lead

   ``automation-v3`` runs the server, a worker, the local client, or scripts
   on this machine.

.. code-block:: text

   Automation Framework

   Usage:
       automation-v3 demo [--path PATH] [--port PORT] [--no-docs] [--debug]
       automation-v3 server [--port PORT] [--dbpath PATH]
                            [--workspace-path PATH] [--reports-path PATH]
                            [--docs-path PATH] [--local-worker] [--config PATH]
                            [--settings PATH] [--debug]
       automation-v3 worker [--port PORT] [--config PATH]
                            [--central-server URL] [--no-http] [--debug]
       automation-v3 run SCRIPT... [--root PATH] [--config PATH]
                         [--env NAME]... [--variation NAME]... [--filter EXPR]
                         [--uut NAME=VERSION]... [--reports-path PATH]
       automation-v3 client [--port PORT] [--workspace-path PATH] [--server URL]
                            [--config PATH] [--data-path PATH] [--debug]
       automation-v3 login --server URL [--email EMAIL]
       automation-v3 logout [--server URL]
       automation-v3 whoami [--server URL]
       automation-v3 builds [--server URL]
       automation-v3 scratch SCRIPT... [--root PATH] [--server URL]
                             [--env NAME]... [--variation NAME]...
                             [--uut NAME=VERSION]...
                             [--no-wait]
       automation-v3 report edit REPORT [--title TEXT] [--number TEXT]
                            [--revision TEXT] [--author TEXT]
                            [--sign ROLE=NAME]... [--applicable DOC]...
                            [--reference DOC]...
       automation-v3 report export REPORT [--out DIR] [--template DIR]
       automation-v3 report reopen REPORT
       automation-v3 requirements import SOURCE... [--spec KEY] [--baseline NAME]
                            [--title TEXT] [--level LEVEL] [--parents KEYS]
                            [--sheet NAME] [--dbpath PATH] [--server URL]
       automation-v3 requirements log [--limit N] [--dbpath PATH]
       automation-v3 requirements history ID [--dbpath PATH]
       automation-v3 requirements diff FROM TO [--spec KEY]
                            [--subsystem NAME] [--dbpath PATH]
       automation-v3 lsp [--scripts PATH] [--dbpath PATH]
       automation-v3 (-h | --help)

   Commands:
       demo                   set up a demo (sample scripts, requirements and
                              these docs) in a fresh folder, and serve it with
                              a worker. Deletes an earlier demo at --path
       server                 serve the web app and the job API, optionally
                              with a worker in the same process
       worker                 take jobs from a server and run them
       run                    run scripts on this machine, without a server
       client                 the local client's web UI, on this machine only:
                              your worktrees' scripts, checked as you write them,
                              run in scratch on the central server (or here,
                              with --config). Sign in first with login
       login                  sign this machine in to a central server: it
                              emails you a link to approve it
       logout                 sign this machine out, and revoke its token
       whoami                 who this machine is signed in as
       scratch                run scripts from your worktree in the central
                              server's scratch space, on its workers: in-work
                              edits included. Waits and prints each step.
                              With --uut NAME=local it uses your local build
                              of NAME, uploading it first if it isn't yet
       builds                 your local builds (see client.json), and whether
                              each is uploaded
       report edit            set a report's document fields: its title,
                              number, revision and author, who signs it, and
                              its applicable and reference documents
       report export          freeze a report and write its PDF and bundle,
                              report-<id>.zip
       report reopen          unfreeze an exported report, so runs can be
                              added to it again
       requirements import    import requirements, in order: DOORS export
                              folders (or zips of them), or a spec as a
                              spreadsheet (CSV, TSV or Excel) or a list, one
                              per line (with --spec). Into the
                              database, or with --server into a central
                              server (admins only)
       requirements log       the latest imports, and what each changed
       requirements history   every change to a requirement, and the
                              baselines it is in
       requirements diff      the requirements added, removed and changed
                              from one context to another: trunk, trunk@N
                              (as of import N), set:NAME (a baseline set)
                              or SPEC@BASELINE
       lsp                    the language server for scripts, on stdin and
                              stdout: errors as you type, completion, hover
                              and signature help, in any editor that speaks
                              the Language Server Protocol. Requirement ids
                              are read from the database, if it is there

   Options:
       -h --help              show this help message and exit
       --port=PORT            tcp port to bind to [default: 8080]
       --dbpath=PATH          path to application database file
                              [default: ./automationv3.db]
       --workspace-path=PATH  path to git repo [default: ./] (not used when the
                              settings name a [git] remote to mirror)
       --reports-path=PATH    directory holding reports and runs
                              [default: ./reports]
       --docs-path=PATH       built HTML documentation to serve at /docs
       --path=PATH            the demo's folder [default: ./demo]
       --no-docs              don't build the documentation
       --central-server=URL   the central server: host:port, or a URL
       --config=PATH          worker config (JSON) naming the environments
                              it hosts
       --settings=PATH        server settings (TOML): sign-in, mail and a git
                              remote to mirror. Without it the server is
                              single-user
       --no-http              run the worker without its status page
       --local-worker         also run a worker inside the server process
                              (hosting the environments in --config)
       --root=PATH            root script path SCRIPTs are relative to
                              [default: ./]
       --server=URL           a central server (default: the one you last
                              signed in to)
       --email=EMAIL          your work email (asked for if not given)
       --no-wait              queue and print the runs' links, without waiting
       --data-path=PATH       where the client keeps its own scratch runs
                              (default: ~/.local/share/automation-v3/client)
       --env=NAME             environment to run in (default: all hosted)
       --variation=NAME       variation to run (default: all)
       --filter=EXPR          EDN predicate selecting variations
       --uut=NAME=VERSION     UUT version to use (default: newest)
       --debug                Flask's development server, with its debugger
                              and reloading on code changes, on 127.0.0.1
                              only [default: false]
       REPORT                 a report's folder (in the reports path)
       --title=TEXT           the report's name, its document's title; or a
                              CSV or list spec's title
       --number=TEXT          the document's number
       --revision=TEXT        the document's revision
       --author=TEXT          the document's author
       --sign=ROLE=NAME       who signs for a role, e.g. "Approved by=J. Doe"
       --applicable=DOC       an applicable document, "NUMBER | REVISION | TITLE";
                              replaces the report's list
       --reference=DOC        a reference document, "NUMBER | REVISION | TITLE";
                              replaces the report's list
       --out=DIR              where to write the bundle (default: the report
                              folder's exports/)
       --template=DIR         the document template (default: the built-in one)
       SOURCE                 an export folder (holding manifest.json) or a
                              zip of one; or a spec's requirements in a .csv,
                              .tsv, .xlsx or .txt (a list), with --spec
       --sheet=NAME           the sheet of an Excel workbook (default: the
                              first)
       --baseline=NAME        the baseline a CSV or list is (default: trunk)
       --level=LEVEL          a CSV or list spec's level: system, segment or
                              software [default: software]
       --parents=KEYS         the specs a CSV or list spec's requirements
                              trace up to, comma separated
       --limit=N              how many imports to show [default: 10]
       --spec=KEY             the spec a CSV or list is; for diff, only
                              this spec's requirements
       --subsystem=NAME       only this subsystem's requirements
       --scripts=PATH         the folder scripts are in (default: the rvts
                              folder of the folder the editor has open, or
                              that folder itself)
cards.heading: Command line

cards.text:
``demo``
--------

Sets up a fresh demo folder (sample scripts, requirements and these docs)
and serves it with a worker in-process. See :doc:`../overview/getting-started`.
cards.heading: ``demo``

cards.text:
``server``
----------

Serves the web app and the job API. ``--workspace-path`` is the git checkout
scripts are read from; ``--reports-path`` is where finished runs are stored.
``--settings`` makes it a central server: sign-in, mail, and a mirror of the
team's git remote instead of ``--workspace-path`` (see
:doc:`../operating/deployment`).
With ``--local-worker`` it also runs a worker in-process, hosting the
environments in ``--config``. ``--docs-path`` serves a build of these docs
at ``/docs``, with a **Docs** link in the navigation.
cards.heading: ``server``

cards.text:
``worker``
----------

Takes jobs from the server at ``--central-server`` and runs them in the
environments named in ``--config``. A central server needs a worker token,
``"token"`` in the config or ``AUTOMATION_WORKER_TOKEN``. See
:doc:`../operating/workers`.
cards.heading: ``worker``

cards.text:
``client``, ``login``, ``logout``, ``whoami``, ``scratch`` and ``builds``
-------------------------------------------------------------------------

The local client, on your own machine (see :doc:`../operating/local-client`).
``login --server URL`` signs this machine in by emailed link, and the rest use
that sign-in. ``client`` serves the web UI for your worktrees on
``127.0.0.1``. ``scratch SCRIPT...`` uploads scripts from your worktree, edits
included, to run in the central server's scratch space, printing each step.
``builds`` lists your local builds and whether each is uploaded.

.. code-block:: bash

   automation-v3 login --server https://automation.example.com
   automation-v3 client --workspace-path ~/work/scripts
   automation-v3 scratch BRA/tc_bra_00004.rst --env sim --uut demo=local
cards.heading: ``client``, ``login``, ``logout``, ``whoami``, ``scratch`` and ``builds``

cards.text:
``run``
-------

Runs scripts on this machine with no server or database. ``SCRIPT`` paths
are relative to ``--root``. It prints each step, writes a normal report
folder under ``--reports-path`` and exits non-zero unless every run passed.

.. code-block:: bash

   automation-v3 run BRA/tc_bra_00004.rst --root test/data/rvts --config test/data/worker.json --variation limp-home --uut demo=1.0.0
cards.heading: ``run``

cards.text:
``requirements``
----------------

Imports and inspects requirements. ``import`` reads each ``SOURCE`` and
imports them in the order given, saying what happened to each spec; a source
with a problem is refused whole and changes nothing. A source is an export
folder (see :doc:`requirements-export`) or a zip of one, or one spec's
requirements as a CSV or a list (see :ref:`flat-requirements`), which needs
``--spec`` to say which spec it is, and may take ``--title``, ``--baseline``,
``--level`` and ``--parents`` (and ``--sheet``, for a workbook). ``log`` lists the latest imports and the requirements each
added, removed or changed; ``history`` follows one requirement through every
import and baseline.

With ``--server URL``, ``import`` uploads each source to a central server
instead, which takes imports from admins only.

``diff`` compares two contexts: ``trunk``, ``trunk@N`` (trunk as of import
``N``), ``set:NAME`` (a baseline set) or ``SPEC@BASELINE``. Each line is a
requirement and what changed: ``added``, ``removed``, or its ``text``,
``metadata``, ``links`` or ``section``.

.. code-block:: bash

   automation-v3 requirements import exports/2026-10-15
   automation-v3 requirements import srs.csv --spec SRS --parents SYS
   automation-v3 requirements diff "set:Release 1" trunk --spec SRS-VM
   automation-v3 requirements history VM-EPS-002
cards.heading: ``requirements``

cards.text:
``lsp``
-------

Runs the language server for scripts on stdin and stdout, which is how
editors start one. It reports the same errors and warnings a script's page
shows, as you type, and completes the names a block can use: blocks,
builtins, the definitions of the script and its ``core.rst`` files, UUT
handles and variation values. Hovering a name says what it is, and typing a
call shows how it is called. In prose, ``:req:`` ids complete, show the
requirement's text on hover, and are flagged when they aren't requirements:
these come from the database at ``--dbpath``, when there is one. The web
app's editor uses the same server.

The scripts root is the ``rvts`` folder of the folder the editor has open,
or that folder itself when it has none; ``--scripts`` names another. See
:doc:`../operating/editor` for setting up an editor.
cards.heading: ``lsp``

cards.text:
Glossary
========

.. glossary::
   :sorted:

   BuildingBlock
      A step scripts call by name, written in Python. See :doc:`../blocks/writing-blocks`.

   closure
      A script plus every ``core.rst`` and import it loaded. Stored with each run.

   ref
      A reference to a value scripts read, wait on and drive, by its path.
      Plugins define their own kinds, and the blocks that reach them. See
      :doc:`../scripts/refs`.

   group
      Refs tested together, such as redundant units: Verify and Wait check
      every member. See :doc:`../scripts/refs`.

   clock
      What a run keeps time by: the wall clock, or a simulation's, as its
      environment says.

   combination
      One (script, environment, variation) a report expects a run of.

   core.rst
      A folder's shared definitions and declarations, loaded by every script below it.

   action
      A block that does something to the system. Fails if it can't.

   assertion
      A block that checks something. Fails when the check comes out false.

   value block
      A block that reads something and gives it back. Reported quietly, with its value.

   cleanup
      What a block registers to run when the script ends, however it ends,
      such as SetFixedValue releasing its value.

   drift
      An environment whose fingerprint no longer matches a run being rerun.

   environment
      Where a script runs, such as a simulator or a bench. Hosted by workers.

   fingerprint
      Facts about an environment, and the framework, that can affect results.

   force mode
      Running a job with its UUTs installed and started fresh.

   handle
      The object bound to a UUT's name that scripts call methods on.

   heal
      The part of a precondition that establishes the state it checks.

   identity
      The hash of a run's closure, variation values, UUT versions and fingerprint.

   precondition
      The state a script needs before its steps run, with an optional heal.

   probe
      Trying a job against the environment as it is, without reinstalling.

   report
      A named, growing collection of runs rolled up to requirements.

   rollup
      Each tracked requirement's state in a report: green, red or partial.

   rvt
      The rst directive holding script code.

   scratch space
      Where scripts under development run, outside any report.

   UUT
      A unit under test, installed into and started in an environment.

   variation
      One way of running a script, binding its variation symbols to values.

   worker
      A process next to the hardware that pulls and runs jobs.
cards.heading: Glossary

cards.text:
Script language
===============

.. rst-class:: lead

   Everything a script can contain, in one place.
cards.heading: Script language

cards.text:
Directives (rst)
----------------

``.. rvt:: [title]``
   A block of script code. Options:

   ``:definitions:``
      The block only defines things; shown collapsed; only before the first
      step.

   ``:variations: name, name``
      The block applies only to these variations.

   With a title, the block's forms are collapsed under it.

``.. rvt-variant::``
   Prose and ``rvt`` blocks that apply only to some variations. Option:
   ``:variations: name, name`` (required).

``:req:`ID```
   References a requirement the script verifies.
cards.heading: Directives (rst)

cards.text:
Forms
-----

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 40 60

   * - Form
     - Kind
   * - ``(def name value)``
     - definition, top level only
   * - ``(defn name [params] body...)``
     - definition, top level only
   * - ``(uut :name)``
     - declaration
   * - ``(environments :name ...)``
     - declaration
   * - ``(import FOLDER)``
     - directive, top level only
   * - ``(variations "sym ..." ["name" [values...] ...])``
     - directive, once per script
   * - ``(Precondition "text" check [:heal ["text"] heal])``
     - precondition, before the first step
   * - anything else in a list
     - a step
cards.heading: Forms

cards.text:
Special forms
-------------

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 40 60

   * - Form
     - Meaning
   * - ``(if test then else?)``
     - conditional
   * - ``(do forms...)``
     - evaluate in order, returning the last
   * - ``(and forms...)``, ``(or forms...)``
     - evaluate left to right only until the result is decided, returning
       that value
   * - ``(let [name value ...] body...)``
     - local bindings
   * - ``(fn name? [params] body...)``
     - a function; ``(fn ([a] ...) ([a b] ...))`` for several arities
   * - ``(quote form)``, ``'form``
     - the form unevaluated; vectors, maps and sets otherwise evaluate their
       items
   * - ``(.method obj args...)``
     - call a method on a Python object
   * - ``(.-attr obj)``
     - read an attribute
   * - ``(step "title" body...)``
     - group the body's block calls under one reported entry
   * - ``(try-ok? form)``
     - true if no block call in it failed, else false; never stops the step
   * - ``(try form default)``
     - the form's value, or the default if a block call in it failed
   * - ``(TBD)``, ``(TBD "text")``
     - a step not written yet (its block's title, or the text, says what
       it will do); true where a value is expected; a run that
       reaches one is incomplete
   * - ``(quietly forms...)``
     - run forms with their block calls left out of the output
cards.heading: Special forms

cards.text:
Built-in functions
------------------

Arithmetic and comparison
   ``+ - * / > < >= <= = not=`` and ``abs``, ``max``, ``min``, ``round``,
   ``expt``, and every function and constant of Python's ``math`` module
   (``sqrt``, ``pi``, ...).

Logic
   ``not``. ``and`` and ``or`` are special forms: they short-circuit.
   ``and`` returns the first falsy value or the last value; with no arguments
   it returns true. ``or`` returns the first truthy value or the last value;
   with no arguments it returns nil. Truthiness keeps the existing rules:
   nil, false, zero and empty collections are falsy.

Sequences
   ``first``, ``rest``, ``cons``, ``append``, ``count``, ``list``, ``map``,
   ``take``, ``cycle``, ``range``, ``partition``, ``apply``, ``nth``,
   ``vector``, ``vec``, ``filter``, ``reduce``.

   These are eager: ``map``, ``filter``, ``take``, ``rest``, ``cons``,
   ``partition``, ``vec`` and ``range`` return EDN vectors, which can be counted, indexed
   and read more than once. ``cycle`` alone is endless; bound it with
   ``take`` before passing it to anything else.

   ``(range end)``, ``(range start end)`` and ``(range start end step)``
   return a finite EDN vector of integers, excluding ``end``. The default
   start is 0 and step is 1; negative steps are allowed, zero is an error.
   Unlike the earlier unbounded counter, ``(range)`` requires a bound and
   ``(range 5)`` is ``[0 1 2 3 4]``.

Maps
   ``assoc``, ``dissoc`` (both return copies), ``get``, ``get-in``,
   ``contains?``, ``keys``, ``vals``. ``get`` takes a map's key, a set's
   member or a sequence's index, and gives nil (or a default) when missing.

Predicates
   ``nil?``, ``some?``, ``number?``, ``symbol?``, ``list?``,
   ``procedure?``, ``eq?``.

Strings and output
   ``str``, ``print``.

Refs
   ``group``, ``same?``, ``ref?``; plugins add their own, such as the
   Vehicle Manager's ``connector``. See :doc:`../scripts/refs`.
cards.heading: Built-in functions

cards.text:
Collection helpers
------------------

``(get collection key default?)``
   Read a map key or a nonnegative sequence index. Missing entries return
   the default, or ``nil``. Existing ``false`` and ``nil`` values are kept.

``(get-in collection [key ...] default?)``
   Follow nested map keys and sequence indexes. An empty path returns the
   original value. A missing part returns the default, or ``nil``.

``(nth collection index default?)``
   Read a zero-based sequence or iterator index. A missing index raises an
   error unless a default is supplied. Negative indexes are missing;
   booleans and noninteger indexes are errors.

``(contains? collection key)``
   Test map/set membership or whether a sequence index exists. This tests
   indexes, not sequence values: ``(contains? [10 20] 1)`` is true,
   ``(contains? [10 20] 20)`` is false.

``(keys map)``, ``(vals map)``
   Return vectors in the map's insertion order.

``(vector value ...)``, ``(vec collection)``
   Construct a vector, or copy/materialize an iterable into one. ``vec``
   on a map gives its keys. It is useful for the iterators returned by
   ``map`` and ``take``.

``(filter predicate collection)``
   Return a vector of items for which the predicate is truthy.

``(reduce function collection)``, ``(reduce function initial collection)``
   Accumulate a result. Without ``initial``, use the first item; on an empty
   collection call the function with no arguments (``(reduce + [])`` is 0).
   With ``initial``, an empty collection returns it.

``keys``, ``vals``, ``vec`` and ``filter`` return EDN vectors, not iterators,
so their results can be counted, reused and shown in reports. ``nil`` is
treated as an empty collection by those functions and by ``reduce``.
cards.heading: Collection helpers

cards.text:
Literals
--------

Besides edn's, time literals: a number with a unit, ``500ms``, ``5s``,
``2min``, ``1h`` (or ``msec``, ``seconds``, ``minutes``, ``hours`` and their
like). Each is a number of seconds that is shown as written.
cards.heading: Literals

cards.text:
Dotted names
------------

A name like ``cpu1.app.mode`` that nothing defines as a whole is a path below
the ref its first part (``cpu1``) is bound to. See :doc:`../scripts/refs`.
cards.heading: Dotted names

cards.text:
Bound names
-----------

While a script runs, these are bound in addition to definitions:

- each variation symbol, to the running variation's value;
- each UUT's name (e.g. ``demo``), to its handle, if it offers one.

``wait-timeout`` and ``wait-every``, if a script or its ``core.rst`` defines
them, are Wait's defaults.
cards.heading: Bound names

cards.text:
Report documents
================

.. rst-class:: lead

   A report's document is reStructuredText: prose, and directives where the
   report's data goes.

Every report has a document, ``report.rst`` in its folder. A report starts
from its workspace template's ``report.rst``. You can then edit it until the
report is frozen. The directives stay in it for good: they're resolved against
the report's data whenever the document is shown or built, and the data they
read travels with the report, so an exported bundle can always be built again.
cards.heading: Report documents

cards.text:
Directives
----------

Each directive writes one part of the document, from a snippet of the same
name (below):

``.. report-identification::``
   What the report is: its id and name, its workspace, its runs, the UUT
   versions and environments they ran on, and the requirements context. An
   exported document adds when it was exported and its bundle.

``.. report-summary::``
   The requirements and combinations by state, with how they're judged.

``.. open-issues::``
   Requirements no script tests yet, and each combination that didn't pass,
   with why.

``.. requirement-results::``
   Each requirement the report tests: its text as the report kept it, its
   verdict, and the combinations covering it.

   ``:group-by:``
      ``subsystem`` (the default) or ``none``.
   ``:subsystem:``
      Only this subsystem's requirements.
   ``:color:``
      Only requirements with this verdict: ``green``, ``red``, ``partial``
      or ``untested``.

``.. results::``
   The latest run of each combination, its outcome and duration.

   ``:script:``
      Only scripts matching this pattern, e.g. ``BRA/*``.
   ``:state:``
      Only combinations in this state, e.g. ``fail``.

``.. reruns::``
   Earlier attempts of each combination, newest first.

``.. failures::``
   For each failing combination: its run, the step it failed at, and the
   message.

``.. report-bundle::``
   What the exported bundle holds, and its manifest's SHA-256.
cards.heading: Directives

cards.text:
Values in prose
---------------

``:report:`name``` writes one value:

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 30 70

   * - Name
     - Value
   * - ``title``, ``number``, ``revision``, ``author``
     - The document's fields.
   * - ``id``
     - The report's id.
   * - ``context``
     - The requirements context the report verifies.
   * - ``runs``
     - How many runs it has.
   * - ``requirements``, ``requirements.green`` (any verdict)
     - How many requirements it tests, in all or with that verdict.
   * - ``combinations``, ``combinations.fail`` (any state)
     - How many combinations it covers, in all or in that state.
   * - ``uut.NAME``
     - The version of a UUT the report runs on.
   * - ``first_run``, ``last_run``
     - When its first run started and its last ended.

For example::

   This report verifies the brake controller, version :report:`uut.brakes`,
   against :report:`context`: :report:`requirements.green` of its
   :report:`requirements` requirements passed.
cards.heading: Values in prose

cards.text:
Snippets
--------

What a directive writes comes from a snippet: a Jinja template that writes
reStructuredText, named after the directive (``report/results.rst`` for
``.. results::``). In a snippet:

- a line starting ``%`` is a Jinja statement (``% for row in rows``), and one
  starting ``%#`` a comment; either line is dropped whole, so blank lines come
  out as written;
- ``{{ value }}`` writes the value as plain text, never markup;
- filters write markup: ``literal``, ``verdict``, ``link(url)``,
  ``requirement`` (a requirement's text), ``indent(n)``, ``verbatim`` (a
  literal block's body), ``heading(char)``, and ``seconds``, ``plural``,
  ``stamp`` for numbers and times;
- ``data`` is the report (``data.combinations``, ``data.requirements``,
  ``data.runs``, ``data.document``, ...), and ``options`` the directive's
  options.

A snippet is looked up in the report template's ``snippets/`` folder first,
then in plugins', then among the built-in ones (in
``automationv3/documents/snippets/``). To change how a part of every report
reads, copy the built-in snippet into your workspace template's
``snippets/report/`` and edit it.
cards.heading: Snippets

cards.text:
How outputs differ
------------------

A snippet writes the same reStructuredText for every output: live pages
render it with docutils, a frozen report's site and PDF with Sphinx. What it
wants shown differently carries a class: ``:verdict:`fail``` (bold text in
an inline classed ``verdict-fail``) and ``.. container:: requirement``. Live
pages and the site style them with CSS; the PDF with the LaTeX commands they
become (``\DUroleverdict-fail``, the ``sphinxclassrequirement`` environment),
which the template's ``latex.tex_t`` defines.
cards.heading: How outputs differ

cards.text:
Requirements export format
==========================

.. rst-class:: lead

   What the DOORS exporter writes and automation imports: a folder holding a
   manifest and one Sphinx source tree per spec. This page is the contract
   between the two; the exporter is a separate application. Without DOORS, a
   spec can be imported from a CSV or a list instead.

An export is a folder. Each run of the exporter writes a new one; automation
imports it with ``automation-v3 requirements import FOLDER``.

.. code-block:: text

   export-2026-10-17/
     manifest.json
     SYS/                  one folder per spec in the manifest
       index.rst
       scope.rst
       images/fig-1.png
     SEG-SPACE/
       index.rst
     SRS-VM/
       index.rst
       executive.rst
       power.rst

An export may hold any number of specs, and the same spec more than once (its
trunk and a new baseline, say), or only baseline sets over baselines imported
before. Specs not in the manifest are not touched by
the import: a folder exporting only ``SRS-VM`` says nothing about ``SYS``.
cards.heading: Requirements export format

cards.text:
The manifest
------------

``manifest.json`` describes the export and each spec in it:

.. code-block:: json

   {
     "format": 1,
     "exporter": {"name": "doors-export", "version": "0.3.0"},
     "exported_at": "2026-10-17T02:00:00Z",
     "specs": [
       {
         "key": "SRS-VM",
         "title": "Vehicle Manager Software Requirements",
         "level": "software",
         "parents": ["SEG-SPACE"],
         "root": "SRS-VM",
         "doors": {"module": "/Platform/Software/SRS VM",
                   "id_source": "Absolute Number"},
         "attributes": {
           "subsystem": {"type": "string"},
           "verification": {"type": "enum",
                            "values": ["Test", "Analysis", "Inspection",
                                       "Demonstration"]},
           "allocation": {"type": "list"},
           "last-modified-by": {"type": "string", "hashed": false}
         }
       },
       {
         "key": "SRS-VM",
         "baseline": "2.1",
         "root": "SRS-VM@2.1",
         "...": "the same fields as above"
       }
     ],
     "baseline_sets": [
       {"name": "Release 2",
        "specs": {"SYS": "1.0", "SEG-SPACE": "1.2", "SRS-VM": "2.1"}}
     ]
   }

``format``
   The version of this contract: ``1``. Automation refuses formats it doesn't
   know.

``exported_at``
   When the exporter read DOORS: ISO 8601 with a time zone
   (``2026-10-17T02:00:00Z``). Needed whenever the export holds a trunk. It
   orders trunk, which only moves forward: an export older than the trunk
   already imported for a spec is refused, so re-running an old pipeline
   can't roll trunk back. What *changed* is still decided by content, never
   by dates.
``exporter``
   Informational: the exporter's name and version.

``specs``
   One entry per spec in the export:

   ``key``
      The spec's short, stable name (``SYS``, ``SEG-SPACE``, ``SRS-VM``).
      Letters, digits, ``-``, ``_`` and ``.``.
   ``title``
      Its name for people.
   ``level``
      Where it sits: ``system``, ``segment`` or ``software``.
   ``parents``
      The keys of the specs its requirements may trace up to. A system spec
      has none.
   ``root``
      The folder, relative to the manifest, holding the spec's Sphinx source,
      with ``index.rst`` at its top.
   ``baseline``
      The DOORS baseline this is, such as ``"2.1"``. Absent for trunk: the
      module's current, unbaselined state.
   ``doors``
      Where it came from: the module's path and which DOORS column gave the
      requirement ids (``id_source``). Informational.
   ``attributes``
      The spec's attribute schema (below).

``baseline_sets``
   DOORS baseline sets: a name, and the baseline of each spec it pins. Each
   pinned baseline must be in this export or imported before. Optional.
cards.heading: The manifest

cards.text:
The spec's documents
--------------------

A spec is a Sphinx source tree, without ``conf.py``: automation supplies the
configuration, the ``requirement`` directive and the theme when it renders
the spec, so every spec looks like the rest of the site. ``index.rst`` holds
the spec's title and a ``toctree`` of its chapters; everything DOORS holds
that isn't a requirement (headings, prose, tables, figures) is written as
ordinary rst, and images go in the tree and are referenced relatively.

Write headings without their DOORS numbers ("Power", not "3.2 Power"):
Sphinx numbers them, and a number that shifts whenever a section is
inserted above would make every requirement below look moved.

Each requirement is a ``requirement`` directive:

.. code-block:: rst

   .. requirement:: VM-EPS-002
      :satisfies: SEG-PWR-004, SEG-PWR-007
      :subsystem: EPS
      :verification: Test
      :allocation: VM, PCDU
      :last-modified-by: jdoe

      The VM shall shed loads in the order of the load shedding table when
      the battery state of charge falls below each of the following
      thresholds:

      - 60%: the payload;
      - 40%: everything except the essential loads.

The argument
   The requirement's id. The spec's ``doors.id_source`` says where the
   exporter took it from: the object's absolute number (with the module's
   prefix) or a column of its own. Ids are unique across every spec; an
   import that would give two specs the same id fails.

``:satisfies:``
   The ids of the parent requirements this one traces up to, comma
   separated. Links are written on the child only, like DOORS out-links;
   automation works out the other direction. A link need not resolve: one
   whose target is missing, or in a spec that isn't one of ``parents``, is
   shown as a trace issue rather than failing the import.

Every other option
   An attribute, named as in the spec's schema. Option names are lower case,
   with ``-`` for spaces (``Last Modified By`` is ``last-modified-by``).

The content
   The requirement's text, in rst: lists, emphasis, notes and tables are all
   fine. It must not be empty.
cards.heading: The spec's documents

cards.text:
Attribute schemas
-----------------

Each spec lists the attributes its requirements may carry. An option not in
the schema, or a value its type doesn't allow, fails the import, so a typo
can't quietly become a new attribute.

``"type"``
   ``string`` (any one-line value), ``enum`` (one of ``"values"``) or
   ``list`` (comma-separated values; their order doesn't matter).
``"hashed"``
   ``false`` for attributes that change without the requirement changing:
   DOORS's Last Modified On and By, Object Number, Created Thru. They are
   kept and shown, but a change to them is not a new version. Default
   ``true``.

An attribute named ``subsystem`` groups requirements on the Requirements
page and in reports. Map whichever DOORS column holds it (Allocation, CSCI,
Subsystem) to ``subsystem``.
cards.heading: Attribute schemas

cards.text:
What makes a change
-------------------

Automation decides what changed by hashing content, so the exporter must be
deterministic: the same DOORS content exported twice must give the same
requirements. It need not give identical bytes. Each requirement is hashed in
four parts:

text
   The plain text of the content, with whitespace collapsed. Markup
   (emphasis, line wrapping, list bullets) doesn't count, so improving the
   RTF conversion doesn't make every requirement look changed; wording does.
metadata
   The hashed attributes and their values.
links
   The ``:satisfies:`` ids, as a set.
section
   The titles of the sections the requirement is in, from its chapter down.
   A requirement moved to another section has moved; one reordered within
   its section has not.

The whole source tree of each spec is kept too, so any version can be shown
exactly as it was.

.. _flat-requirements:
cards.heading: What makes a change

cards.text:
A CSV or a list
---------------

Without DOORS, or before its exporter is ready, a spec can come from a
spreadsheet or a text file instead. Each file is one spec; importing it names
the spec (``--spec SRS`` on the command line, or the Spec field on the
Imports page), and may give its title, baseline, level (software by default)
and parents. It is read into the same form as an export, so everything works
the same: re-importing an edited file is a new trunk, with its history,
changes and suspects, and ``--baseline 1.0`` freezes a version.

A **spreadsheet** (``.csv``, ``.tsv`` with tabs, or an Excel workbook,
``.xlsx``) has a header row, then a row per requirement. Each column has a
role: the id, the text, the ids it satisfies, its section, an attribute, or
ignored. On the command line the roles are guessed from the headers; the
Imports page guesses too, then lets you change them (see
:doc:`../operating/requirements`). A workbook's sheet is ``--sheet NAME``, by
default the first with anything on it. Reading workbooks needs ``openpyxl``
(``pip install automation-v3[xlsx]``).

.. code-block:: text

   id,text,satisfies,section,subsystem,verification
   SRS-001,The VM shall shed loads below 40%.,SYS-12,Power,EPS,Test
   SRS-002,The VM shall report the state of charge.,,Power,EPS,Test
   SRS-003,The VM shall keep time.,SYS-3,Time,TIM,Analysis

``id`` and ``text``
   Needed. Guessed from headers like *ID*, *Req ID*, *Object Identifier*,
   and *Text*, *Requirement*, *Object Text*. An id has no spaces or commas,
   and is unique in the file; a text
   may span lines (quoted, as spreadsheets save it), and a blank line in it
   starts a new paragraph.
``satisfies``
   Optional (*Parent*, *Parent Requirements*, *Traces to*): the ids it
   traces up to, separated by commas, semicolons or line breaks. They should
   be in the specs given as ``parents``, or show as trace issues.
``section``
   Optional: a heading to file it under, as a spec document's headings do.
   Moving a requirement to another section is a change; reordering rows is
   not.
Every other column
   An attribute, kept as text, named after its header in lower case with
   ``-`` between words (*Verification Method* is ``verification-method``). A
   ``subsystem`` attribute groups requirements as it does for DOORS.

A **list** (``.txt``) has one requirement per line: its id (a colon after it
is fine), then spaces or a tab, then its text. Blank lines, and lines starting with
``#``, are skipped.

.. code-block:: text

   # The VM SRS, until DOORS
   SRS-001  The VM shall shed loads below 40%.
   SRS-002: The VM shall report the state of charge.

The text is plain: characters reStructuredText would read as markup, like
``*`` or a leading ``-``, are kept as written. Save files as UTF-8 (Excel's
*CSV UTF-8*). A file with a problem (a missing id or text, an id twice) is
refused whole, with every problem and its line listed.

Each requirement needs an id that stays the same from one import to the
next: it is how history, ``:req:`` references and reports find it. A list of
bare texts can't be imported, as an id made up from a line's position or its
words would change whenever the file did.
cards.heading: A CSV or a list

cards.text:
Checklist for the exporter
--------------------------

- One folder per run, with ``manifest.json`` at its top, ``"format": 1``,
  and ``exported_at`` the time DOORS was read, in UTC.
- One entry per spec and version: trunk with no ``baseline``, each DOORS
  baseline with its name. A baseline, once imported, can't change: exporting
  ``SRS-VM 2.1`` again with different content is an error.
- Every spec a Sphinx tree under its ``root``, ``index.rst`` at the top, no
  ``conf.py``.
- Headings without their DOORS numbers.
- One ``requirement`` directive per requirement object, with its id, its
  ``:satisfies:`` links and its attributes as options.
- Every attribute in the spec's schema; volatile ones ``"hashed": false``.
- Deterministic output: nothing that changes between runs of unchanged
  content (no timestamps in the documents).
- DOORS baseline sets in ``baseline_sets``.
cards.heading: Checklist for the exporter

cards.text:
Requirements
============

.. rst-class:: lead

   Requirements come from DOORS as specs: a system spec, segment specs and
   software requirements specs, traced to each other and versioned by
   content. Automation keeps every version, so it can show what a spec said
   at any baseline, what changed since, and which tests that touches.
cards.heading: Requirements

cards.text:
Specs and traces ---------------- A spec is a document: requirements, and the headings, prose, tables and figures around them. Each has a key (``SRS-VM``), a level and the specs above it: .. mermaid:: :caption: The demo's specs, and the way their requirements trace flowchart BT vm["SRS-VM
Vehicle Manager SRS"] -- satisfies --> space["SEG-SPACE
Space segment spec"] vmc["SRS-VMC
Vehicle Management
Computer SRS"] -- satisfies --> ground["SEG-GROUND
Ground segment spec"] space -- satisfies --> sys["SYS
System spec"]:::accent ground -- satisfies --> sys A requirement traces up with ``:satisfies:``, naming the requirements above it that it helps meet. The link is written on the child; automation works out the other direction (what satisfies this?) and finds trace issues: a link to an id that doesn't exist, or to a spec that isn't one of the spec's parents. Ids are unique across all specs. Requirements carry attributes (verification method, allocation, status), declared per spec; the ``subsystem`` attribute groups them on the Requirements page and in reports. How specs arrive is :doc:`requirements-export`: a folder from the DOORS exporter, imported with ``automation-v3 requirements import``.
cards.heading: Specs and traces

cards.text:
Trunk and baselines
-------------------

Each spec has a **trunk**, its current state in DOORS, exported as often as
daily, and **baselines**, frozen versions such as ``2.1``. A **baseline set**
(a release) pins one baseline of each spec, as DOORS baseline sets do.

Importing trunk compares it with the trunk before, requirement by
requirement, and logs what changed. Trunk only moves forward: an export
older than the trunk already imported is refused. Importing a baseline stores it once and
never again, and refuses different content under the same name. An import of
unchanged content changes nothing, so the exporter can run on a schedule and
the log only grows when DOORS did.
cards.heading: Trunk and baselines
Versions are by content

cards.text:
History and differences
-----------------------

From those versions automation answers:

- **A requirement's history**: each import that changed it, and which parts,
  and the baselines it appears in.
- **What changed between two points**: two baselines, two baseline sets, a
  baseline and trunk, or two trunk imports; for a whole spec, a subsystem or
  everything. Requirements added, removed, and changed (and how).
- **What changed recently**: the trunk import log, newest first.
cards.heading: History and differences

cards.text:
Changes reach tests
-------------------

When a requirement's text changes, everything below it may need another
look: the requirements that satisfy it, and the scripts that reference it
with ``:req:``. Both become **suspect** until someone reviews them; a
script's review is recorded for its workspace against the text it was
reviewed against, so it becomes suspect again only on the next change.

Each workspace verifies one context: trunk, or a baseline set. Its
requirement texts, coverage and suspects are those of that context. A run
records the version of each requirement it verified, so a report can tell a
pass against today's text from a pass against an older one.
cards.heading: Changes reach tests

cards.text:
Using them
----------

:doc:`../operating/requirements` covers importing from CI, the Requirements
pages, setting the context a workspace verifies, and reviewing suspects.
cards.heading: Using them

cards.text:
Block reference
===============

.. rst-class:: lead

   Every BuildingBlock scripts can call, documented by the block itself:
   how to call it, and what it does.

Each entry is generated from the block: the calls come from its ``usage()``
and the text from its docstring (see :ref:`documenting-blocks`). In a usage,
``name?`` is optional and ``name...`` or ``name ...`` repeats.

.. building-blocks::
cards.heading: Block reference

cards.text:
Composing blocks
================

.. rst-class:: lead

   Blocks can be called anywhere in a step: at the top level, inside a
   ``defn``, a ``let`` or an ``if``. Wherever the call is, it reports and fails
   the same way. Three forms change that, and they say so where they are used.
cards.heading: Composing blocks

cards.text:
Wherever it is called
---------------------

A block call is reported with its own result, and a failure stops the
statement (and so the script) right there. A ``defn`` is transparent: the
blocks it calls report as calls of the step that called it.

.. code-block:: clojure

   (defn start-and-check [pressure]
     (StartDemo {:mode :normal :readings {:brake-pressure pressure}})
     (Verify (reading :brake-pressure) <= max-pressure))

   (start-and-check 60)

If ``StartDemo`` fails, ``Verify`` never runs.
cards.heading: Wherever it is called

cards.text:
``(step "title" body...)``
--------------------------

Groups the block calls of its body under one entry in the report, with the
title, nested beneath it. A failure inside still stops it, and the step
around it. It gives the body's value.

.. code-block:: clojure

   (defn brakes-hold [pressure]
     (step "Brakes hold the pressure"
       (StartDemo {:mode :normal
                   :readings {:brake-pressure pressure}})
       (Verify (reading :brake-pressure) <= max-pressure)))

Use it for a procedure that should read as one step in a report.
cards.heading: ``(step "title" body...)``

cards.text:
``(try-ok? form)``
------------------

Runs the form and gives ``true`` if no block call in it failed, ``false`` if
one did, without stopping the step. Use it to branch on whether something
works:

.. code-block:: clojure

   (if (try-ok? (Verify (reading :brake-pressure) <= 50))
     (set-reading :brake-pressure 70)
     (clear-faults))

The calls inside are still reported, marked as suppressed (shown as true or
false rather than passed or failed).
cards.heading: ``(try-ok? form)``

cards.text:
``(try form default)``
----------------------

Like ``try-ok?``, but gives the form's value, or ``default`` (evaluated) if a
block call in it failed:

.. code-block:: clojure

   (def version (try (InstalledVersion :demo) "unknown"))

``try-ok?`` and ``try`` only catch block failures. A mistake in the script's
own code, such as an unknown name, still stops the step.
cards.heading: ``(try form default)``

cards.text:
Only the last check counts
--------------------------

To run several checks and let only the last decide, suppress the earlier ones
explicitly:

.. code-block:: clojure

   (step "Settles within limits"
     (try-ok? (Verify (reading :brake-pressure) <= 60))   ; may overshoot
     (Wait 2)
     (Verify (reading :brake-pressure) <= 60))
cards.heading: Only the last check counts

cards.text:
``(quietly forms...)``
----------------------

Runs the forms with their block calls left out of the output. Calls still run
and fail as usual. Use it for housekeeping that would clutter the report.

.. code-block:: clojure

   (quietly
     (StartDemo {:mode :normal}))
cards.heading: ``(quietly forms...)``

cards.text:
Summary
-------

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 30 35 35

   * - Called in
     - Reported
     - A failure
   * - top level, ``defn``, ``let``, ``if``...
     - as a call of the step
     - stops the step
   * - ``step``
     - nested under its title
     - stops it, and the step
   * - ``try-ok?``, ``try``
     - marked as suppressed
     - gives ``false``, or the default
   * - ``quietly``
     - not shown
     - behaves as where it is called
cards.heading: Summary

cards.text:
Definitions and shared code
===========================

.. rst-class:: lead

   Name values and functions once, and share them through the folder tree.
cards.heading: Definitions and shared code

cards.text:
The two definitions
-------------------

``(def name value)``
   Names a value.

   .. code-block:: clojure

      (def max-pressure 100)

``(defn name [params] body...)``
   Names a function. Called as a step, it passes unless a block it calls
   fails; to check what it returns, assert it: ``(Verify (demo-in-mode?
   :normal))``.

   .. code-block:: clojure

      (defn demo-in-mode? [m]
        (and (.running demo) (= (.mode demo) m)))

   A function that calls blocks can group them in the report with ``step``:

   .. code-block:: clojure

      (defn brakes-hold [pressure]
        (step "Brakes hold the pressure"
          (StartDemo {:mode :normal
                      :readings {:brake-pressure pressure}})
          (Verify (reading :brake-pressure) <= max-pressure)))

Definitions are never reported as steps, and only appear at the top level of
a ``core.rst`` or a script, never inside another form (a ``defn``, a
``let``...). That is what lets every name a script uses be checked before it
runs; see :ref:`checked-before-running`.
cards.heading: The two definitions

cards.text:
A script's definitions section
------------------------------

Definitions that belong to one script go in ``rvt`` blocks marked
``:definitions:``, before any step. The web app shows them collapsed, so the
page leads with the test itself:

.. code-block:: rst

   .. rvt::
      :definitions:

      (def stop-pressure 70)

A definitions block can be limited to some variations, to override a value for
those variations only; see :ref:`scoped-definitions`.

.. _core-chain:
cards.heading: A script's definitions section

cards.text:
The ``core.rst`` chain ---------------------- Every folder, including the workspace root, may hold a ``core.rst`` of shared definitions and declarations. A script loads the ``core.rst`` of every folder from the root down to its own: .. mermaid:: :caption: Each script loads the chain from the root to its folder; an import only adds names flowchart TB root["core.rst
(environments :sim) (uut :demo)
(def max-pressure 100)"] bra["BRA/core.rst
(def max-pressure 80)
(defn brakes-hold …)"] brakes["BRA/tc_bra_00001.rst
max-pressure is 80"]:::accent fuel["FUEL/tc_fuel_00001.rst
(import BRA)
max-pressure is 100, and brakes-hold"]:::accent root -- shadowed by --> bra bra -- loaded by --> brakes root -- loaded by --> fuel bra -. "import: adds brakes-hold,
keeps max-pressure" .-> fuel Inner definitions shadow outer ones, so ``BRA/`` tightens the limit for every brake script. A ``core.rst`` is a document too: explain what each definition is for, and the workspace renders it like any other page. A ``core.rst`` may only contain documentation, ``def``, ``defn``, ``uut`` and ``environments``.
cards.heading: The ``core.rst`` chain

cards.text:
Imports
-------

``(import FOLDER)`` loads another folder's ``core.rst`` definitions:

.. code-block:: clojure

   (import BRA)

Imports only add definitions. They never override a name the script's own
``core.rst`` chain defines, so importing ``BRA`` into a fuel script gets
``brakes-hold`` without changing the fuel folder's ``max-pressure``. Imports
must be at the top level of an ``rvt`` block.
cards.heading: Imports

cards.text:
Scripts and definitions together
--------------------------------

The ``core.rst`` chain, imports and the script's definitions section load
before any step runs. A definition placed later in a script, between steps,
takes effect where it is, like a step: steps above it can't use it (the static
check says so), and if it fails to evaluate the script ends in error there.

.. _checked-before-running:
cards.heading: Scripts and definitions together

cards.text:
Checked before running
----------------------

Because definitions only live at the top level, the names a script can use
are known without running it: builtins, the ``core.rst`` definitions, the
script's own definitions in order, UUT handles and variation symbols (bound
after the definitions section loads), and the parameters and ``let`` names
in scope. A name that is none of these is an error before the script can be
queued, shown by the statement it is in, with a suggestion when one is
close. A ``core.rst`` function's names are checked when a script can call
it, since a ``core.rst`` may serve scripts that bind more than this one
(``in-variation-mode?`` uses ``mode``, which only scripts with variations
bind).

A script's own definition of a name shadows any block of the same name, so a
script can stand in for a block while it is being developed.
cards.heading: Checked before running

cards.text:
Writing scripts that read well
==============================

.. rst-class:: lead

   A script is reviewed as a document. These features exist so the rendered
   page reads like a test procedure, not like code.
cards.heading: Writing scripts that read well

cards.text:
Write the prose first
---------------------

Say what the test checks and why before showing how. The prose between
``rvt`` blocks is always shown, whichever variation is selected, so it should
make sense on its own. Use headings ("Requirements", "Setup", "Steps") to give
long scripts a shape the page can be skimmed by.
cards.heading: Write the prose first

cards.text:
Title the blocks
----------------

An ``rvt`` block can take a title. A titled block collapses its forms behind
the title, so the page reads as a list of named steps. The titles are the
procedure, so they can come first, with ``(TBD)`` standing in for steps not
written yet (see :doc:`planning`):

.. code-block:: rst

   .. rvt:: Apply the variation's brake pressure

      (TBD)

   .. rvt:: Verify the brake pressure stays within the safe limit

      (TBD)

When a step is written, its block keeps the title. Expanding the title shows
the forms. On a run page the title carries the block's overall result and
duration. Untitled blocks show their steps at the top level, as before.
cards.heading: Title the blocks

cards.text:
Describe heals
--------------

Give a precondition's heal a description, so the page says what it does in
words:

.. code-block:: clojure

   (Precondition "Demo running in normal mode"
     (demo-in-mode? :normal)
     :heal "Start the demo in normal mode"
     (start-demo :normal))
cards.heading: Describe heals

cards.text:
Keep variation-specific prose with its code
-------------------------------------------

Use ``.. rvt-variant::`` so the explanation of a variation-specific check is
hidden along with the check when another variation is selected. See
:doc:`variations`.
cards.heading: Keep variation-specific prose with its code

cards.text:
Let blocks render themselves
----------------------------

Blocks can render their arguments readably: ``StartDemo`` shows its
configuration as a table, ``Verify`` as a sentence. Prefer a block with a good
rendering over a ``defn`` that hides the same logic. If a block shows as raw
code and could read better, ask its developer to give it an ``as_rst``
(:doc:`../blocks/rendering`).
cards.heading: Let blocks render themselves

cards.text:
Keep definitions out of the way
-------------------------------

Put a script's own definitions in a ``:definitions:`` block at the top, where
the page collapses them, and shared ones in ``core.rst`` with prose explaining
them.
cards.heading: Keep definitions out of the way

cards.text:
Your first script
=================

.. rst-class:: lead

   A script is an rst document with code in it. Everything outside the
   ``rvt`` blocks is documentation.

.. code-block:: rst

   ================
   Brake Monitoring
   ================
   Checks the brake pressure stays under the limit.

   Requirements
   ------------
   1. :req:`VMCBRA00001`

   .. rvt::
      :definitions:

      (def target 60)

   Steps
   -----

   .. rvt::

      (set-reading :brake-pressure target)
      (Verify (reading :brake-pressure) <= max-pressure)
cards.heading: Your first script

cards.text:
The parts
---------

The title
   The document title is the script's name on every page.

``:req:`ID```
   Each ``:req:`` role links the script to a requirement. Reports roll the
   script's results up to these requirements, and the Requirements page lists
   the script under each one. Put them anywhere in the prose; a numbered
   "Requirements" section is the convention.

   Aim for one requirement per script, so a failure points at one
   requirement and a requirement's status reads straight off its scripts. A
   requirement can have several scripts (say, one for the cases that need
   their own run); when splitting isn't practical, list them all.

``.. rvt::``
   A block of script code. Each top-level form in it is one statement:
   a step, a definition, or a directive. Blocks run in document order, so a
   script reads top to bottom as it executes.

``:definitions:``
   Marks a block that only defines things. The web app shows it collapsed,
   and it may only appear before the first step. See :doc:`definitions`.

Steps
   ``(set-reading :brake-pressure target)`` calls a function defined in a
   ``core.rst``; ``(Verify ...)`` calls the ``Verify`` BuildingBlock. Each
   is reported as a step with its own pass/fail badge and duration. See
   :doc:`steps`.
cards.heading: The parts

cards.text:
Where things come from
----------------------

``set-reading``, ``reading`` and ``max-pressure`` aren't defined in this
script. They come from the ``core.rst`` files in the script's folder and every
folder above it (see :ref:`core-chain`). ``Verify`` is a BuildingBlock in the
``core`` plugin. ``demo``, the handle used inside ``reading``, is bound to the
UUT the script tests, declared in the root ``core.rst``:

.. code-block:: clojure

   (environments :sim)
   (uut :demo)

A script can override those declarations with its own ``(environments ...)``
or ``(uut ...)``.
cards.heading: Where things come from

cards.text:
What is a script, and what isn't
--------------------------------

Any ``.rst`` file with at least one ``rvt`` block is a script. Plain documents,
such as a folder's ``README.rst``, are rendered as documentation only. A
``core.rst`` is never a script; it holds shared definitions and declarations.
cards.heading: What is a script, and what isn't

Checking a script
-----------------

The web app lints a script when it renders and before it queues. Lint errors
appear at the top of the script page and stop it being queued. Common ones:

- a ``Precondition`` after a regular step;
- a ``:definitions:`` block after a step, or one that contains a step;
- a ``:variations:`` option naming a variation the script doesn't declare;
- an ``import`` that isn't at the top level;
- a ``core.rst`` containing anything but definitions and declarations.

cards.text:
Writing scripts
===============

.. rst-class:: lead

   A guide for test authors: how a script is put together, from a single
   Verify to variations, preconditions and shared definitions.

A script is an ``.rst`` file in a workspace. You write it in your editor,
commit it to git, and the web app renders, lints and queues it. Nothing here
needs Python: the steps call BuildingBlocks that block developers provide, and
the definitions you write yourself are in a small Lisp.

While a script is under development, run it from the
:doc:`scratch space <../operating/scratch>` (it uses your working tree,
uncommitted edits included) or from the command line with
``automation-v3 run``.
cards.heading: Writing scripts

cards.text:
In this section
---------------

:doc:`first-script`
   The anatomy of a script: title, requirements, ``rvt`` blocks, steps.

:doc:`steps`
   What makes a step, how it passes or fails, and the forms you can write.

:doc:`definitions`
   ``def`` and ``defn``; the ``core.rst`` chain and imports; checks before
   running.

:doc:`variations`
   Running one script several ways, and blocks and prose that only apply to
   some of them.

:doc:`preconditions`
   Stating the state a script needs, and how to heal into it.

:doc:`composing`
   Blocks inside definitions: ``step``, ``try-ok?``, ``try`` and ``quietly``.

:doc:`documenting`
   Making the rendered script read well: titles, variants and prose.

:doc:`planning`
   Writing a test's flow first with ``(TBD)`` steps, for review, and
   filling it in later.

:doc:`blocks`
   Every BuildingBlock you can call, with its usage and documentation.

A complete example
------------------

This is ``BRA/tc_bra_00004.rst`` from the sample set. Every piece of it is
explained in the pages that follow.

.. literalinclude:: ../../test/data/rvts/BRA/tc_bra_00004.rst
   :language: rst
cards.heading: A complete example

cards.text:
Planning a test before writing it
=================================

.. rst-class:: lead

   Write a test's flow first, as titled groups of steps described in words,
   so it can be reviewed as a whole. Then replace the words with real steps,
   one group at a time.
cards.heading: Planning a test before writing it

cards.text:
Placeholder steps
-----------------

``(TBD)`` is a step that isn't written yet. Give each one an ``rvt`` block
of its own, titled with what the step will do:

.. code-block:: rst

   .. rvt:: Set the autopilot engage switch to ON

      (TBD)

   .. rvt:: Verify the autopilot reports engaged within 1 frame

      (TBD)

   .. rvt:: Verify the active lateral mode is roll hold

      (TBD)

The script page shows the titled blocks collapsed, as always, and tags each
one that holds a ``TBD`` with *TBD*, so the page reads as the test's
procedure: reviewers see each step and what it will do, which are still to
be written, and the requirements and variations around them. When a step is written, its block keeps the title.

Where a step can't have a block of its own, give the ``TBD`` the words
instead: ``(TBD "what the step will do")``. That is the way inside code (an
``if``, a precondition's check) and among the steps of a
table block (see :doc:`variations`), which runs its block's steps once per row.

Everything else works as usual around them. A ``TBD`` can sit in a ``defn``
in a ``core.rst`` (a shared step nobody has written yet), in a precondition's
check or heal, or among real steps. Where a value is expected, a ``TBD`` comes
out true, so the flow after it runs too.
cards.heading: Placeholder steps

cards.text:
Running a test that isn't finished
----------------------------------

A script with ``TBD`` steps can be queued and run, for example in the
:doc:`scratch space <../operating/scratch>`. The real steps run; each ``TBD``
is reported as :status:`to do` and the run goes on. A run that reached any
``TBD`` can't pass: if nothing else stopped it, its outcome is
**incomplete**, and the requirements it covers roll up partial, never green.

The static check counts them, as a warning on the script page: *10 steps
are still to be written (TBD)*.
cards.heading: Running a test that isn't finished

cards.text:
Check what you can now
----------------------

Even before the system under test can be driven, a test's own data can be
checked. The Vehicle Manager examples in the sample set state the expected
result of each variation in a table, and their first step checks that table
against the requirement, written once as a function in the folder's
``core.rst``:

.. code-block:: clojure

   (Verify (transition-allowed? from to) = allowed)

That step is real from the start: a mistake in the table fails the run long
before anyone flies it.
cards.heading: Check what you can now

cards.text:
Examples
--------

The ``VM`` folder of the sample set holds tests written this way, for the
Vehicle Manager of a satellite platform: 66 scripts across ten subsystems
(executive, telecommand, telemetry, modes, FDIR, attitude control, power,
thermal, time and storage), testing the 64 requirements of
the ``SRS-VM`` spec in ``test/data/doors/specs``. The mode, power and
telecommand tests have since been written in full, against a simulated
Vehicle Manager; the others are still flows and come out incomplete. Compare
the two kinds side by side: the flow below, and ``VM/EPS/tc_eps_002.rst``
written out.
